    Cleanup

    • The training and processing jobs have already ended; there is nothing to stop. Check Training jobs and Processing jobs anyway: nothing should say InProgress.
    • Delete what you no longer need from s3://<your-bucket>/badger-scribe/ (the models/ and predictions/ prefixes). The adapter is small, but prediction outputs accumulate across runs.
    • Stop your notebook instance. It is a CPU instance at five cents an hour, a charge that goes unnoticed for a semester.

    Bonus exercises

    Not part of the class session. Exercise 1 relaunches the class job with one change and takes about an hour of GPU time; Exercise 2 is arithmetic only.

    Challenge

    Exercise 1: Image resolution

    Relaunch the same job with "max_pixels": 2560 * 28 * 28 (~2 megapixels, twice the 1280 * 28 * 28 of the class run) and the job name badger-{username}-churro-lora-2ep-2mp-{run_id}, with a fresh run_id. Before it starts, write down your prediction for its billable time, and raise max_run to match: the 65-minute cap was set for the 1-megapixel job. Then compare train_minutes and seconds_per_page in the two summaries, and the before/after CER. Did the extra pixels help?

    Time per page roughly doubles: the sequence is twice as long and attention cost grows faster than linearly. On these scans the strokes are legible well below 1 megapixel, so the extra pixels mostly buy tokens that carry no information, and CER usually moves very little. Resolution is the first thing to lower when a fine-tune is over budget, and the first to raise if the model is misreading small characters such as the ½ fractions.

    Challenge

    Exercise 2: Cheaper per run, or just faster?

    ml.g6e.xlarge (one L40S, 48 GB) costs $2.61/h on the Instances for ML page, 1.85x the price of ml.g5.xlarge, and runs this workload roughly 2.5–3x faster. It also has twice the GPU memory, so batch_size can be 2 or 4 instead of 1, which uses the GPU more efficiently.

    Using the Step 0 phase table, estimate the cost of the class job on ml.g6e.xlarge. Then do the same for the homework run (25 min of training, 34 min of scoring, 6 min of startup and upload on the g5). Which phase does not get faster, and when does the faster instance save money?

    Startup and upload (~6 min, $0.26 at $2.61/h) do not speed up: the container pull and the S3 copies are the same on any instance. For the class job, training drops from ~12 to ~4 minutes and the ~14 minutes of scoring to ~5, so the job is about 15 minutes and ~$0.65: a little less than the $0.75 g5 run. At this size the two are nearly a wash, because the fixed overhead is a third of the faster job.

    The homework run on the g5 is 25 + 34 + 6 = 65 minutes, about $1.50. On the g6e at 2.5–3x: ~9 minutes of training, ~12 of scoring, the same 6 of overhead, about 27 minutes and ~$1.20. The longer the GPU work, the more the faster card saves: the g5 bill grows linearly with pages and passes while the g6e bill grows at about two-thirds of the slope. The g6e only loses on a job so short that the fixed overhead dominates, a 5-minute smoke test, say.

    Compare the cost per run, not the hourly rate: the fixed overhead is a larger share of it on faster hardware. The catch is quotas: the account needs a service quota for ml.g6e.xlarge training jobs, and those often default to zero.

    Key Points
    • Fine-tuning cost is GPU-hours × hourly rate, and GPU-hours scale with model size × tokens × epochs × attempts. The same recipe runs from under a dollar (3B, LoRA, a few hundred pages) to tens of thousands (70B, full fine-tune, days on multi-GPU nodes). Starting from a model that already knows most of the task is the biggest saving available.
    • Training jobs, not GPU notebooks, are the safe way to run it: they end, max_run guarantees it, a unique job_name prevents a second copy launching by accident, and checkpoints synced to S3 mean a killed job costs an epoch, not the run. Interrupting a notebook cell does not stop a job.
    • Estimate before launching (startup overhead + pages × epochs × seconds per page, at the instance’s rate), then compare to BillableTimeInSeconds.
    • Image resolution (max_pixels) and epochs change cost by multiples; the instance size changes it by 5–45x, which is right when the model does not fit on one GPU and waste when it does.
    • Score the holdout at the end of every epoch: the curve, not a rule of thumb, says how many passes were worth paying for. Measure the gain on the same held-out pages before and after, with the task’s own metric, and a page-level holdout is optimistic when the real test is split by document.

    Content from Hyperparameter Tuning in SageMaker: Neural Network Example

    Last updated on 2026-10-27 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 60 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How can we efficiently manage hyperparameter tuning in SageMaker?
    • How can we parallelize tuning jobs to optimize time without increasing costs?

    Objectives

    • Set up and run a hyperparameter tuning job in SageMaker.
    • Define ContinuousParameter and CategoricalParameter for targeted tuning.
    • Log and capture objective metrics for evaluating tuning success.
    • Optimize tuning setup to balance cost and efficiency, including parallelization.
    • Read back what a whole tuning job cost from its child training jobs.

    Open the notebook from: /ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/notebooks/09_Hyperparameter-tuning.ipynb. Select the conda_pytorch kernel.

    Hyperparameter tuning in SageMaker

    The PyTorch episode trained one neural network with a learning rate and an epoch count chosen by hand. Those settings change the result, and choosing them by hand means launching a series of experiments and keeping track of their scores yourself. SageMaker’s hyperparameter tuner does that for us. We say which settings may vary, how a good result is measured, and how many training jobs we are willing to pay for.

    Each trial is an ordinary SageMaker training job, launched from the controller notebook on its own instance. The tuner changes the hyperparameters between trials and compares the validation metric they report. That makes the search easier to run, but it does not make it free. Ten trials are ten training jobs on the bill, and what keeps a tuning job cheap is the choice of ranges and the number of models trained. We begin with a single trial to check the configuration before paying for a larger search, the same test-first pattern as the training episodes.

    The experiment

    We reuse the Titanic network and training data from the PyTorch episode and tune two settings, epochs and learning_rate. One is picked from a short list of values, the other sampled from a continuous range. Two settings are enough to see the mechanics without a new dataset or model. In your own work you may tune more.

    There are three pieces to connect. An estimator says how each model is trained, a search space says what may change, and a validation metric tells SageMaker which trials did better. The tuner then bounds the search with the total number of trials, max_jobs, and how many run at once, max_parallel_jobs. Afterwards we read the results, add up the billed compute time, and evaluate the chosen model on the test data.

    Set up the project folder

    Start in the Titanic project folder, as in the previous episodes:

    PYTHON 

    # The Titanic project folder from the S3 episode, beside the lesson clone: downloads and outputs land here, not in the repository
!mkdir -p /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/titanic
%cd /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/titanic
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "/home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts")
import helpers

    Define the training job

    We begin with a PyTorch estimator like the one in the previous episode. It names the training script, the instance, the input paths and the metric to record. When it is handed to the tuner, SageMaker uses it as the template for every trial and substitutes new values for the hyperparameters being searched. The training script does not change.

    We’ll use our notebook instance name again to label the training jobs launched in this episode

    PYTHON 

    import boto3

notebook_instance_name = 'SinkOrSwim-DoeJohn' # adjust to your notebook name. we'll use this variable to name the training jobs launched by the tuner.

# the following code just verifies you have the right name for your notebook instance
region = boto3.Session().region_name  # inherited from the notebook instance; do not hard-code a region
sagemaker_client = boto3.client('sagemaker', region_name=region) # Initialize SageMaker client
response = sagemaker_client.describe_notebook_instance(NotebookInstanceName=notebook_instance_name) # Describe the notebook instance

# Display the status and instance type
print(f"Notebook Instance '{notebook_instance_name}' status: {response['NotebookInstanceStatus']}")
local_instance = response['InstanceType']
print(f"Instance Type: {local_instance}")

    Cost tracking: As in every training episode, we explicitly tag each training job at launch time. This ensures that compute usage is traceable to a project, a purpose, and a human-readable name, even after the job has completed. Tags on the HyperparameterTuner are copied to every child training job it launches, so we only need to set them once, on the tuner (we also set them on the estimator so a plain .fit() on it is tagged too).

    PYTHON 

    name = "DoeJohn" # replace with your name
project = "SinkOrSwim"   # your challenge: WattBot2026, BadgerScribe, BadgerCode, BrainDecoding, PoisonedWell or SnapshotWI; SinkOrSwim is the workshop itself
purpose = "Tuning"        # one of: Storage, Notebook, Training, Tuning, Inference

job_tags = [
    {"Key": "Name", "Value": name},
    {"Key": "Project", "Value": project},
    {"Key": "Purpose", "Value": purpose},
]
helpers.check_launch(job_tags)   # the account's rules, checked here first: AWS's own refusal does not say which rule
print(f"Name: {name}, Project: {project}, Purpose: {purpose}")

    Next, we’ll configure the baseline estimator that we plan to do hyperparameter search on.

    Every price in this episode is from the Instances for ML page, us-east-1 on-demand; the tuning job’s cost is that rate times the sum of the child jobs’ billable minutes.

    PYTHON 

    import sagemaker
# range types for the search: ContinuousParameter (float range), IntegerParameter (whole-number range), CategoricalParameter (explicit list)
from sagemaker.tuner import HyperparameterTuner, IntegerParameter, ContinuousParameter, CategoricalParameter
from sagemaker.pytorch import PyTorch
from sagemaker.inputs import TrainingInput
from sagemaker import get_execution_role

# Initialize role, bucket, and SageMaker session variables
role = get_execution_role()
bucket_name = 'sinkorswim-doejohn'  # replace with your S3 bucket name
session = sagemaker.Session()
s3 = boto3.client('s3')
print("Role:", role)
print("Region:", session.boto_region_name)

# Define instance type/count we'll use for training
instance_type="ml.m5.large"
instance_count=1 # always start with 1; tuning parallelism comes from max_parallel_jobs, not instance_count
price_per_hour = 0.115 # ml.m5.large, us-east-1 on-demand (2026-10-16), from the Instances for ML page; check it for your region

# The runtime cap, in seconds: SageMaker stops the job and releases the instance when it is reached. Set it a little above the estimate;
# the estimate here is three or four minutes, so 20 minutes leaves room for a slow container pull without letting a hung job bill for hours.
max_run = 20*60 # 20 minutes

# Define the PyTorch estimator with entry script and environment details
pytorch_estimator = PyTorch(
    base_job_name=f"{notebook_instance_name}-nn",   # who + which model; the tuner appends its own suffix to each child job
    max_run=max_run, # in seconds; always include (max 48 hours)
    entry_point="/home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/train_nn.py",  # Your script for training
    role=role,
    tags=job_tags,  # tags a plain .fit() on this estimator; the tuner below sets its own
    instance_count=instance_count,
    instance_type=instance_type,
    framework_version="2.3",  # if a job fails with an image error, check with: sagemaker.image_uris.retrieve("pytorch", region, version="2.3", py_version="py311", image_scope="training", instance_type="ml.m5.large")
    py_version="py311",
    # the Regex pulls the number out of each "validation:accuracy = 0.8123" line the script prints; SageMaker records it as the metric
    metric_definitions=[{"Name": "validation:accuracy", "Regex": "validation:accuracy = ([0-9\\.]+)"}],
    hyperparameters={
        "train": "/opt/ml/input/data/train/train_data.npz",  # SageMaker will mount this path
        "val": "/opt/ml/input/data/val/val_data.npz",        # SageMaker will mount this path
        "epochs": 100, # Placeholder initial value. Will be overridden by the tuning values tested
        "learning_rate": 0.001 # Placeholder initial value. Will be overridden by the tuning values tested
    },
    output_path=f"s3://{bucket_name}/tuning/",   # every child job's model.tar.gz lands here, in your bucket
    sagemaker_session=session,
)

    Define the search space

    In SageMaker, you must explicitly define ranges for any hyperparameters you want to tune. SageMaker supports ContinuousParameter, IntegerParameter and CategoricalParameter types:

    • ContinuousParameter allows SageMaker to dynamically sample numeric values within a specified range, making it ideal for broad, exploratory tuning. The total number of values tested can be controlled through the upcoming max_jobs parameter, which defines how many different combinations SageMaker will evaluate.
    • IntegerParameter does the same for whole-number settings such as a batch size or layer width.
    • CategoricalParameter specifies exact values for SageMaker to test, which is useful when you want the model to only try a specific set of options.

    By default, SageMaker uses Bayesian optimization, adjusting future selections based on previous results to efficiently find optimal values. You can also set the strategy to “Random” for uniform sampling across the range, which is effective in larger or more exploratory search spaces. Random search usually needs more jobs to find as good a configuration, and the bill is the number of jobs. Generally, we recommend sticking with the default setting.

    PYTHON 

    # Hyperparameter tuning ranges
hyperparameter_ranges = {
    "epochs": CategoricalParameter([100, 1000, 10000]),       # exact values to try, nothing in between; adjust as needed
    "learning_rate": ContinuousParameter(0.001, 0.1),  # any float in this range; the Bayesian strategy picks where to sample
}

    Configure the tuner

    The HyperparameterTuner brings the estimator and the search space together. It also needs an objective. Here it maximizes validation:accuracy, which the training script prints and SageMaker reads out of the log. The strategy chooses which configurations to try, max_jobs caps how many training jobs are launched in total, and max_parallel_jobs says how many run at once. Parallel trials finish sooner, and each one still bills its own instance.

    Tuning gains are usually marginal past 20 to 30 configurations, and the search space is where the money goes: a published range for the parameters that matter beats a wide search over all of them.

    We first set both limits to one. That single trial checks that the script, the metric extraction, the input files and the permissions all work before we pay for a search.

    PYTHON 

    # Tuner configuration
tuner = HyperparameterTuner(
    base_tuning_job_name=f"{name}-nn-tune"[:20],   # tuning job names are capped at 32 characters and the SDK appends a 12-character timestamp, so the base gets at most 20; child jobs are named <tuning job>-001-<hash>
    estimator=pytorch_estimator,  # the blueprint: every child training job is this estimator with different hyperparameters
    # same regex as the estimator; the value it captures is what the tuner compares across child jobs
    metric_definitions=[{"Name": "validation:accuracy", "Regex": "validation:accuracy = ([0-9\\.]+)"}],
    objective_metric_name="validation:accuracy",  # Ensure this matches the metric name exactly (the "Name" above)
    objective_type="Maximize",                   # Specify if maximizing or minimizing the metric
    hyperparameter_ranges=hyperparameter_ranges,  # the search space defined above
    strategy="Bayesian",  # Default setting (recommend sticking with this!); can adjust to "Random" for uniform sampling across the range
    max_jobs=1,                # Always start with 1 job for debugging purposes. Adjust based on exploration needs (keep below 30 to be kind to environment). 
    max_parallel_jobs=1,         # Always start with 1 for debugging purposes. Recommended to keep this value <= 4 since SageMaker tests values dynamically.
    tags=job_tags,               # propagated to every training job the tuner launches
)

    Check how the objective metric is recorded

    A tuner needs a number from every trial. train_nn.py prints the validation accuracy during training, and the estimator’s metric_definitions regex pulls that value out of the job’s log. The name in the log line, in the metric definition and in the tuner’s objective_metric_name have to agree, or SageMaker has nothing to compare the trials on.

    Note: It’s best to use an if statement to only print out metrics periodically (e.g., every 100 epochs), so that your print time does not eat up too much of your training time. Printing every epoch is a measurable share of a step this small. On the flipside of this, you don’t want to print metrics so infrequently that you lose resolution in the monitored validation accuracy. Choose a number between 100-1000 epochs or divide your total epoch count by ~25 to yield a reasonable range.

    PY 

    if (epoch + 1) % 100 == 0 or epoch == epochs - 1:
    print(f"validation:accuracy = {val_accuracy:.4f}", flush=True)  # Log for SageMaker metric tracking

    Paired with this, our metric_definitions above uses a regular expression "validation:accuracy = ([0-9\\.]+)" to extract the val_accuracy value from each log line. This regex specifically looks for validation:accuracy =, followed by a floating-point number, which corresponds to the format of our log statement in train_nn.py.

    Launch the first trial

    Now we give the tuner the training and validation .npz files the PyTorch episode saved to S3. The two TrainingInput channels map those files to the paths train_nn.py expects. tuner.fit() starts the tuning job. SageMaker launches one training job with one configuration from the search space and records the validation metric it reports. With max_jobs=1 this is a test of the setup, not yet a search.

    Estimate first: one child job is the same three billable minutes as the PyTorch episode’s CPU job, almost all of it startup, so about $0.01.

    If the launch is refused with an AccessDeniedException ending in explicit deny, the account’s checks are the cause: a missing tag, an instance type outside the lesson’s list, or a resource kind the lesson never creates; the first training episode’s callout If the launch is refused says what to look at.

    PYTHON 

    # Define the input paths
train_input = TrainingInput(f"s3://{bucket_name}/train_data.npz", content_type="application/x-npz")
val_input = TrainingInput(f"s3://{bucket_name}/val_data.npz", content_type="application/x-npz")

import time as t

# Launch the hyperparameter tuning job (blocks until the single job has finished)
start_time = t.time()
tuner.fit({"train": train_input, "val": val_input})
print(f"Hyperparameter tuning job finished in {t.time() - start_time:.1f} seconds (wall-clock, including instance startup)")

    Monitor the tuning job

    While the above cell runs, we can check on the progress by visiting the SageMaker Console and finding the “Training” tab located on the left panel. Click “Hyperparameter tuning jobs” to view running jobs.

    What did that cost?

    The money is spent by the training jobs the tuner launches, and that is where SageMaker records billable time. We bring back job_cost_report() from the previous episodes and run it over every child job of the tuner. The list of child jobs comes from tuner.analytics().dataframe() (one row per training job, with its hyperparameters and final objective value).

    PYTHON 

    def job_cost_report(job_name: str, price_per_hour: float):
    desc = session.sagemaker_client.describe_training_job(TrainingJobName=job_name)
    if "BillableTimeInSeconds" not in desc:   # the job has not finished: no bill yet
        print(f"{job_name}: status {desc['TrainingJobStatus']}; billable time and the model path appear once it is Completed")
        return desc
    n = desc["ResourceConfig"]["InstanceCount"]
    billable = desc["BillableTimeInSeconds"] * n
    wall = (desc["TrainingEndTime"] - desc["CreationTime"]).total_seconds()   # launch request to end, including unbilled provisioning
    print(f"{job_name}: status {desc['TrainingJobStatus']}, wall-clock {wall/60:.1f} min, billable {billable/60:.1f} min on {n} instance(s), cost ${billable/3600*price_per_hour:.3f} at ${price_per_hour}/h")
    print(f"    model: {desc['ModelArtifacts']['S3ModelArtifacts']}")   # the model.tar.gz this job uploaded to output_path
    return desc

def tuning_cost_report(tuner, price_per_hour):
    """Call job_cost_report on every training job the tuner launched and print the total."""
    jobs_df = tuner.analytics().dataframe()  # one row per child training job: its hyperparameters, FinalObjectiveValue and TrainingJobName
    total_billable = 0
    for job_name in jobs_df["TrainingJobName"]:
        desc = job_cost_report(job_name, price_per_hour)
        total_billable += desc["BillableTimeInSeconds"] * desc["ResourceConfig"]["InstanceCount"]
    total_cost = total_billable / 3600 * price_per_hour
    print(f"Tuning job {tuner.latest_tuning_job.name}: {len(jobs_df)} training jobs, {total_billable/60:.1f} billable min, ${total_cost:.3f} total")

tuning_cost_report(tuner, price_per_hour)

    Scaling up our approach

    If all goes well, we can scale up the experiment with the below code. In this configuration, we’re scaling up the search by allowing SageMaker to test more hyperparameter configurations (max_jobs=10) while setting max_parallel_jobs=2 to manage parallelization efficiently. With two jobs running at once, SageMaker will be able to explore potential improvements more quickly than in a fully sequential setup, while still dynamically selecting promising values as it learns from completed jobs. SageMaker’s Bayesian optimization uses the completed trials to choose the next ones, so it spends fewer jobs on unpromising combinations. Setting max_parallel_jobs higher than 2-4 reduces tuning efficiency, as SageMaker’s ability to learn from completed jobs decreases when too many jobs run simultaneously.

    With this approach, SageMaker is better able to refine configurations without overloading resources or risking inefficient exploration, making max_parallel_jobs=2 a solid default for most use cases.

    Estimate first: 10 child jobs at roughly 3 billable minutes each is about 30 billable minutes on ml.m5.large, so about $0.06 in total. Wall-clock is five rounds of two jobs, so expect 15-20 minutes. Write both numbers down; the bill below comes in under them.

    PYTHON 

    import time as t

# Configuration variables
max_jobs = 10
max_parallel_jobs = 2

# Define the Tuner configuration
tuner = HyperparameterTuner(
    base_tuning_job_name=f"{name}-nn-tune"[:20],   # tuning job names are capped at 32 characters and the SDK appends a 12-character timestamp, so the base gets at most 20; child jobs are named <tuning job>-001-<hash>
    estimator=pytorch_estimator,
    metric_definitions=[{"Name": "validation:accuracy", "Regex": "validation:accuracy = ([0-9\\.]+)"}],
    objective_metric_name="validation:accuracy",  # Ensure this matches the metric name exactly
    objective_type="Maximize",                   # Specify if maximizing or minimizing the metric
    hyperparameter_ranges=hyperparameter_ranges,
    max_jobs=max_jobs,
    max_parallel_jobs=max_parallel_jobs,
    tags=job_tags,
)

# Track start time
start_time = t.time()

# Launch the hyperparameter tuning job
tuner.fit({"train": train_input, "val": val_input})

# Calculate runtime
runtime = t.time() - start_time

# Print confirmation with runtime and configuration details
print(f"Tuning runtime: {runtime:.2f} seconds, Instance Type: {instance_type}, Max Jobs: {max_jobs}, Max Parallel Jobs: {max_parallel_jobs}")

    Monitoring tuning

    While the above cell runs, we can check on the progress by visiting the SageMaker Console and finding the “Training” tab located on the left panel. Click “Hyperparameter tuning jobs” to view running jobs.

    • Initial Jobs: SageMaker starts by running only max_parallel_jobs (2 in this case) as the initial batch. As each job completes, new jobs from the remaining pool are triggered until max_jobs (10) is reached.
    • Job Completion: Once the first few jobs complete, SageMaker will continue to launch the remaining jobs up to the maximum of 10, but no more than two at a time.

    Once it has finished, the cost report for all 10 child jobs:

    PYTHON 

    tuning_cost_report(tuner, price_per_hour)

    Our run finished in 9.3 minutes of wall-clock and billed 14.1 minutes in total, $0.03: half the estimate. Read the per-job lines and the reason is visible. The first two child jobs billed about 3 minutes each, like every job so far. The other eight billed about 1 minute each. A tuning job keeps its instances between child jobs, so jobs 3 through 10 ran on the two instances that were already up, with the container pulled and the data downloaded. The startup overhead that dominates a single small job was paid twice, not ten times.

    More jobs in parallel

    Bayesian optimization chooses each job’s values from the results so far. With max_parallel_jobs well below max_jobs, later jobs learn from earlier ones; with all ten at once, nothing has finished when the values are chosen, and the search is a random one. The All at once challenge below measures what that does to the result, the wall-clock and the bill.

    Extracting and evaluating the best model after tuning

    Tuning takes about 10 minutes. After SageMaker completes the hyperparameter tuning job, the results, including the trained models for each configuration, are stored in an S3 bucket. The steps to locate and evaluate the best model on test data:

    1. Understanding the folder structure:
      • Each child job uploads its model to the estimator’s output_path, under its own job name: s3://{bucket}/tuning/{job_name}/output/model.tar.gz. Each model is compressed as a .tar.gz file containing the saved model parameters.
    2. Retrieve and load the best model:
      • Using the tuner.best_training_job() method, you can get the name of the best-performing job.
      • From there, retrieve the S3 URI of the best model artifact, download it locally, and extract the files for use.
    3. Prepare test data for final assessment of model generalizability
      • Using the scaler that was fit on the training data.
    4. Evaluate the model on test data:
      • Once extracted, load the saved model weights and evaluate the model on your test dataset to get the final performance metrics.

    The code:

    View best model details and storage info

    We can easily view the best hyperparameters from the tuning procedure…

    PYTHON 

    # 1. Get the best training job from the completed tuning job
best_job_name = tuner.best_training_job()  # the child job with the highest validation:accuracy
print("Best training job name:", best_job_name)

# 2. Use describe_training_job to retrieve full details, including hyperparameters...
best_job_desc = session.sagemaker_client.describe_training_job(TrainingJobName=best_job_name)
best_hyperparameters = {k: v for k, v in best_job_desc["HyperParameters"].items() if k in hyperparameter_ranges}   # the record also carries the SDK's own sagemaker_* entries
print("Best hyperparameters:", best_hyperparameters)

# ...  and model URI (location on S3)
best_model_s3_uri = best_job_desc['ModelArtifacts']['S3ModelArtifacts']  # the model.tar.gz that job uploaded when it finished
print(f"Best model artifact S3 URI: {best_model_s3_uri}")

    Retrieve and load best model

    Download the winning job’s model.tar.gz and unpack it; SageMaker packs whatever the script saved to /opt/ml/model into that archive.

    PYTHON 

    import tarfile

# Download and extract the model artifact: SageMaker packs whatever the script saved to /opt/ml/model into model.tar.gz
local_model_path = "best_model.tar.gz"
model_bucket, model_key = best_model_s3_uri.split('/')[2], '/'.join(best_model_s3_uri.split('/')[3:])  # s3://bucket/key -> bucket, key
s3.download_file(model_bucket, model_key, local_model_path)

# Extract the model files from the tar.gz archive
with tarfile.open(local_model_path, 'r:gz') as tar:
    tar.extractall()
print("Best model downloaded and extracted.")

    Prepare test set as test_data.npz

    In the PyTorch episode, we converted our train dataset into train/validate subsets, and saved them out as .npz files for efficient processing. We’ll need to preprocess our test data the same way to evaluate it on our model.

    Preprocessing lives in a function so that the test set is transformed exactly as the training set was. We’ll import our preprocessing function from train_nn.py, and pass it the scaler that was fit on the training data (saved as scaler.joblib in the previous episode). Calling preprocess_data(test_df) without the scaler would fit a new one on the test set and transform the features differently from what the model saw in training.

    PYTHON 

    !pip install scikit-learn   # train_nn.py imports it; not in the notebook kernels

    Fetch the test CSV and the training-set scaler, transform the test rows the same way the training rows were, and save the arrays.

    PYTHON 

    import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import joblib
from train_nn import preprocess_data

# Fetch the test CSV and the training-set scaler from S3 (both uploaded in earlier episodes)
s3.download_file(bucket_name, "titanic_test.csv", "titanic_test.csv")
s3.download_file(bucket_name, "scaler.joblib", "scaler.joblib")
scaler = joblib.load("scaler.joblib")  # the StandardScaler fit on the training data in the PyTorch episode

# Preprocess test data with the same scaler used for training
test_df = pd.read_csv("titanic_test.csv")
X_test, y_test, _ = preprocess_data(test_df, scaler=scaler)  # transform only; passing the scaler stops it refitting on test data

# Save processed data for testing
np.savez('test_data.npz', X_test=X_test, y_test=y_test)

    Evaluate the model on test data

    Rebuild the network from the script’s class, load the saved weights, and measure accuracy on the test set.

    PYTHON 

    from train_nn import TitanicNet
from train_nn import calculate_accuracy
import torch

# Load the model (saved as 'nn_model.pth' by train_nn.py)
model = TitanicNet()
model.load_state_dict(torch.load("nn_model.pth", map_location="cpu"))
model.eval()

# Load test data
test_data = np.load("test_data.npz")
X_test = torch.tensor(test_data['X_test'], dtype=torch.float32)
y_test = torch.tensor(test_data['y_test'], dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(1)

# Evaluate the model on the test set
with torch.no_grad():
    predictions = model(X_test)
    accuracy = calculate_accuracy(predictions, y_test)
    print(f"Test Accuracy: {accuracy:.4f}")
    Challenge

    All at once

    Rerun the 10-job search with max_parallel_jobs=10 (equal to max_jobs). Before you launch it, predict what changes in (a) total cost, (b) wall-clock time, and (c) the quality of the search. Then run it and check (a) and (b) with tuning_cost_report() and the runtime print.

    PYTHON 

    tuner_parallel = HyperparameterTuner(
    base_tuning_job_name=f"{name}-nn-tune"[:20],   # tuning job names are capped at 32 characters and the SDK appends a 12-character timestamp, so the base gets at most 20; child jobs are named <tuning job>-001-<hash>
    estimator=pytorch_estimator,
    metric_definitions=[{"Name": "validation:accuracy", "Regex": "validation:accuracy = ([0-9\\.]+)"}],
    objective_metric_name="validation:accuracy",
    objective_type="Maximize",
    hyperparameter_ranges=hyperparameter_ranges,
    max_jobs=10,
    max_parallel_jobs=10,
    tags=job_tags,
)

start_time = t.time()
tuner_parallel.fit({"train": train_input, "val": val_input})
print(f"Tuning runtime: {t.time() - start_time:.2f} seconds with max_parallel_jobs=10")
tuning_cost_report(tuner_parallel, price_per_hour)
print("Best objective, sequential-ish run:", tuner.analytics().dataframe()["FinalObjectiveValue"].max())
print("Best objective, all-parallel run:  ", tuner_parallel.analytics().dataframe()["FinalObjectiveValue"].max())
    • Cost: higher, not the same. Our all-parallel run billed 27.5 minutes ($0.05) against 14.1 minutes ($0.03) for the two-at-a-time run. Ten instances each pull the container and download the data, so the startup overhead is paid ten times; with two at a time it was paid twice and the other eight child jobs reused warm instances. (If your account has a quota on concurrent ml.m5.large training instances, the request may be rejected or throttled, which is the practical limit on this approach.)
    • Wall-clock: roughly one job’s duration. Our run took 4.3 minutes against 9.3, so about twice as fast, not five times: the two-at-a-time run’s later jobs were short because they skipped startup.
    • Search quality: with all 10 launched at once, the Bayesian strategy has no completed results to learn from, so the 10 configurations are effectively a random sample of the space. On a 2-parameter problem this small you will usually see a similar best objective either way; on a larger search space with more jobs, the sequential-ish run tends to find a better configuration for the same number of jobs.
    Challenge

    Tune the batch size too

    Suppose you want to add batch_size to the search as IntegerParameter(16, 256). What has to change in train_nn.py for that to do anything, and what has to change in the notebook?

    The tuner can only vary what the script reads. Right now train_nn.py has no --batch_size argument and trains on the full dataset every epoch (one model(X_train) call per epoch), so a batch_size hyperparameter would be passed on the command line, rejected by argparse, and the job would fail. Three changes are needed:

    1. In train_nn.py: add parser.add_argument('--batch_size', type=int, default=64), pass it to train(), and replace the full-batch step with a mini-batch loop, for example by wrapping the tensors in a TensorDataset and iterating over a DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True) inside each epoch (with optimizer.zero_grad(), forward, loss, backward() and step() per batch).

    PY 

    parser.add_argument('--batch_size', type=int, default=64)
...
loader = DataLoader(TensorDataset(X_train, y_train), batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True)
for epoch in range(epochs):
    model.train()
    for xb, yb in loader:
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = criterion(model(xb), yb)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

    1. In the estimator: add a placeholder "batch_size": 64 to hyperparameters, so the argument is always passed.

    2. In the ranges: add "batch_size": IntegerParameter(16, 256) to hyperparameter_ranges.

    Two side effects: an epoch now takes several optimizer steps instead of one, so the same epochs values train for longer (consider shrinking the epochs choices), and the search space has grown, so 10 jobs will cover it less well; 20-30 would be a reasonable budget, which at these prices is still well under a dollar.

    Key Points
    • Tuner = estimator + ranges + objective: A HyperparameterTuner wraps an ordinary estimator; the script only has to print the objective metric in a format the metric_definitions regex can capture.
    • Start with one job: max_jobs=1, max_parallel_jobs=1 first, to catch script and configuration errors before paying for a search.
    • Parallelism buys time, not quality: Cost is per child training job; max_parallel_jobs changes wall-clock time and, with the Bayesian strategy, how much each job can learn from the ones before it. 2-4 parallel jobs is a good default.
    • Tags propagate from the tuner: tags on the tuner are copied to every child training job.
    • Read the bill from the child jobs: SageMaker bills per second of BillableTimeInSeconds x instance count on each training job; container pull and data download are inside that number and dominate short jobs.
    • Transform the test set with the training scaler: Load the saved scaler and pass it to preprocess_data(test_df, scaler=scaler); never refit on test data.

    Content from Overview of RAG Workflows on AWS

    Last updated on 2026-10-28 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 15 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?
    • What are the four ways to run inference on AWS, and which does a RAG pipeline need?
    • Why is Bedrock the default, and when is SageMaker the right choice instead?
    • How do the billing models differ, and what does it cost to forget to shut something down?

    Objectives

    • Explain that RAG trains nothing, so running one does not need a GPU of your own.
    • Name the four ways to run inference on AWS and what each one bills for.
    • Say why pay-per-token Bedrock is the default for most research RAG work.
    • Say when self-managed GPU compute (Processing jobs, notebook GPUs, endpoints) is worth it.
    • Weigh the cost and control trade-offs that decide which to use.

    Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) on AWS

    Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a pattern where you retrieve relevant passages from your own documents and then generate an answer from them. The model is used, not changed. No weights are updated and no training job runs, so the documents can change every week and nothing has to be retrained. Using a trained model to get an output from it, a prediction, an embedding or an answer, is called inference, and everything in this part of the lesson is inference. The example throughout is WattBot, a question-answering challenge over a corpus of research papers on AI and energy.

    There are four ways to run inference on AWS. Call a model through Bedrock’s managed API, run it in a Processing job that ends on its own, load it on a GPU notebook instance, or deploy it as an inference endpoint. This episode compares the four, says why Bedrock is the one to start with, and sets up the episodes that follow, which build the same RAG pipeline in three of these ways and weigh the trade-offs of each.

    What is RAG?

    A language model cannot reliably answer questions about documents it has never seen. RAG connects the model to a collection of material you control. You break the documents into passages, turn each passage into a vector with an embedding model, and keep the vectors so you can search them later. When someone asks a question, you embed the question with the same model and find the passages whose vectors are most similar. Those passages go to a generation model together with the question, and it writes an answer grounded in what was retrieved, citing the passages that support it. When the evidence is not there, a well-built pipeline says so instead of guessing.

    So there are two model calls, and neither is training. The embedding model is called once per chunk when the corpus is indexed and once per question. The generation model is called once per question. Both are inference with no state between calls, so neither needs a GPU of your own. The rest of the pipeline, preparing documents, searching vectors, assembling prompts and scoring answers, is ordinary Python. That code stays the same while the place the models run changes, which is what the next three episodes show.

    Bedrock is the default for inference

    For most RAG pipelines, and for inference in general, Amazon Bedrock is the fastest and most cost-effective starting point on AWS. Bedrock serves embedding and generation models (Amazon Titan, Anthropic Claude, DeepSeek, Meta Llama and others) through pay-per-token APIs. Your retrieval code, chunking, indexing, similarity search, evaluation, stays yours and runs on a cheap CPU notebook or a laptop. Only the two model calls go to Bedrock.

    The difference is in how each one bills.

    Bedrock (managed API) SageMaker GPU instance / endpoint
    Billing unit Per token processed Per second while the instance runs, at an hourly rate
    Cost while idle $0: nothing runs between calls The full hourly rate, around the clock, used or not
    What you have to remember The per-token price before a big batch; route calls through a tagged profile Stop or delete the instance, every time
    Model updates AWS and the provider You: containers, CUDA, GPU memory
    Model choice A curated catalog, proprietary models included Any open-weight model you can load

    Self-hosting on SageMaker gives you control over the weights, the libraries and the hardware, which matters for a specific open-weight model or your own fine-tune. The trade is that a rented GPU bills while the instance runs, whether or not it is generating answers, and research work is mostly occasional experiments, not a steady stream of requests. A GPU instance is a rental whose meter runs until you turn it off, and forgetting to is the most common way a research team spends its cloud budget on nothing. Bedrock has no such failure. Stop calling it and you stop paying.

    What forgetting costs

    A GPU notebook instance left running after you close your laptop (on-demand prices at the time of writing; the instances page has the current ones):

    Instance GPU $/hour Forgotten overnight (12 h) Forgotten over a weekend (64 h) Forgotten for a month (730 h)
    ml.g4dn.xlarge 1 × T4 (16 GB) $0.74 ~$9 ~$47 ~$540
    ml.g5.xlarge 1 × A10G (24 GB) $1.41 ~$17 ~$90 ~$1,030
    ml.g5.2xlarge 1 × A10G (24 GB) $1.52 ~$18 ~$97 ~$1,110
    ml.g6e.xlarge 1 × L40S (48 GB) $2.61 ~$31 ~$167 ~$1,906
    ml.p4d.24xlarge 8 × A100 (40 GB) $25.25 ~$303 ~$1,616 ~$18,430

    Against that, the whole WattBot pipeline of this lesson on Bedrock, with DeepSeek V3 for generation (the Bedrock pricing page has current per-token prices) and Titan Text Embeddings V2 ($0.02 per million tokens):

    Step Rough volume Cost
    Embed ~9,000 chunks (~2.4M tokens) 2.4M input tokens ~$0.05
    Answer and explain the 220 answerable training questions (two calls each, ~1.5K-token prompts) with DeepSeek V3 650K in / 40K out ~$0.50
    Total about $0.55

    One forgotten weekend on the cheapest GPU instance costs more than fifty full runs of the pipeline on Bedrock; a forgotten weekend on the ml.g6e.xlarge the optional GPU-notebook episode uses costs more than a hundred.

    Callout

    Where Bedrock falls short

    • Model choice. You can only call models in the catalog. If the work depends on a specific open-weight model, your own fine-tune, or changes to the model’s internals, you host it yourself.
    • Very large batches. Embedding tens of millions of chunks with a small open model can be cheaper per unit on a short-lived GPU job than per token. Do the arithmetic before assuming either way.
    • Access and regions. Some models have to be enabled in the console first, and the catalog differs by region. Check before a workshop or a deadline.
    • Quotas. On-demand throughput is rate-limited per model and per account. For a large batch, use the batch inference API or request a quota increase instead of retrying against the limit.
    • Data handling. Bedrock does not train on your prompts and keeps data in the region, or within the US when a us. cross-region profile is used; your institution’s policy on sending documents to a hosted API still applies.
    • Cost tracking takes one extra step. On-demand calls carry no tags. To attribute spend to a project you route calls through a tagged application inference profile (the Tagging section below, and the Bedrock episode). Set up once; skip it and the usage is anonymous on the bill.

    Four ways to run inference on AWS

    The four differ less in what the model computes than in how long the hardware stays rented. Here they are in the order to try them.

    1. Amazon Bedrock, the default

    Call the embedding and generation models from your pipeline. You keep the retrieval logic; AWS keeps the models. You pay per token, nothing runs between calls, and there is nothing to shut down. Bedrock is also where proprietary models such as Claude are available without a separate contract.

    Use it for: any RAG system where a catalog model will do, from prototypes and course projects to research tools and production chatbots.

    2. SageMaker Processing jobs

    For a large corpus, or for an open-weight model Bedrock does not carry, run the embedding and the batch generation as jobs instead of against a live model. A Hugging Face Processing job starts a GPU instance, loads the model, works through all the chunks or questions, writes the results to S3 and ends. The GPU exists only while the job runs, so you get a self-managed model without the risk of forgetting to stop it. This is the safest way to use a GPU on SageMaker.

    The cost is latency. A job takes several minutes to start, so this is for work done once and used many times, not for answering one question at a time.

    Use it for: embedding a large corpus with an open model, periodic batch regeneration, or research that needs a model Bedrock does not offer.

    3. A GPU notebook instance

    For models up to about 70B you can choose a GPU instance (an ml.g5.xlarge, say), load the embedding and generation models in the notebook, and run RAG end to end there. It is the simplest setup to follow, and the best way to learn what happens inside a RAG pipeline, because every step is a line of Python you can inspect.

    It is also the most expensive way to run RAG and the easiest to get wrong. The GPU bills by the hour from the moment the instance starts until you stop it, through every stretch spent downloading PDFs, chunking text, reading results or at lunch. It is the route most often forgotten, because a notebook instance looks like a workspace, not a running job. If you use it:

    • Treat it as a learning exercise, not a way to deploy anything.
    • Stop the instance the moment you are done, and check its status on the Notebook instances page.
    • Set an AWS Budget alert, and consider a lifecycle configuration that stops idle notebooks.
    • For larger models the hourly rate ($25 an hour for a p4d.24xlarge; the Instances for ML page has the list) becomes the limit quickly.

    Use it for: walking through RAG step by step, debugging a model before packaging it as a job, or short experiments where you stay at the keyboard.

    4. SageMaker inference endpoints

    For an application that needs interactive, low-latency answers (an API, a chatbot, a dashboard) from a model you host yourself, deploy the embedding and generation models as SageMaker inference endpoints and call them from your retrieval service. You control the model, the scaling and the hardware.

    It is also the most expensive option when traffic is low or bursty, because you pay for capacity that stays up when nobody is asking, the same always-on problem as a notebook GPU, now by design and without end. Before choosing it, ask whether Bedrock already serves a model that will do; it gives the same interactive latency with no idle cost. Endpoints are the answer only when the model itself is why Bedrock will not work.

    Use it for: production systems with steady traffic that need a custom or open-weight model. The lesson does not build one.

    Bedrock charges per call, a Processing job charges for one finite run, and a notebook or an endpoint charges for as long as it is left running. Those lifecycles, not the RAG algorithm, decide which to use.

    Every billable resource needs its own tags

    Cost tracking in this workshop relies on three tags, Name, Project and Purpose, so that Cost Explorer can split the shared bill by challenge. Tags never propagate. Tagging your notebook instance tags the notebook instance and nothing else. Every other resource you create is a separate line on the bill, anonymous unless you tag it when you create it.

    Resource What it bills How it gets tagged
    Notebook instance Hourly, while running Tags you set in the console when creating it
    S3 bucket Storage + requests Tags you set in the console when creating it
    Training / tuning job Per second while the job runs, at an hourly rate tags= argument on the estimator or tuner, every job
    Processing job Per second while the job runs, at an hourly rate tags= argument on the processor, every job
    Inference endpoint Hourly, while deployed tags= argument on deploy()
    Bedrock on-demand call Per token Cannot be tagged directly. Create an application inference profile with tags and pass its ARN as modelId instead of the model ID

    Three things follow:

    1. Each job gets its own tags. A SageMaker job launched from a tagged notebook does not inherit the notebook’s tags. Pass tags=job_tags on every estimator, tuner and processor, as the training, tuning and Processing-job episodes do. Vary Purpose per job so the bill says what the money went to.
    2. Bedrock is tagged through a profile, not a call. invoke_model and converse have no tags parameter. An application inference profile is a free wrapper around one model that carries tags; usage routed through it is attributed to those tags. One profile per base model, so one for the embedding model and one for the generation model. Bedrock’s tag format is lowercase key/value where SageMaker’s is Key/Value; the tag names are the same.
    3. Only the three approved keys count. Name, Project and Purpose, with that spelling and capitalisation; the bill ignores any other key, for the reason the S3 episode gives.

    Which to use

    Your situation Route
    You need to embed and query a document collection and a catalog model (Titan, Claude, Llama, …) will do Bedrock
    You want an interactive chatbot or API over your documents Bedrock
    You need a specific open-weight model and the work is batch (embedding a corpus, bulk generation) Processing jobs
    You are learning how RAG works, or debugging a model step by step Notebook GPU, stopped when you leave
    You need interactive serving of a model Bedrock does not offer, with steady traffic Inference endpoint

    If in doubt, Bedrock. Its worst case is a somewhat higher per-token bill; the worst case on the other routes is a four-figure invoice next month.

    Callout

    The order of the hands-on episodes

    The next two episodes build RAG on Bedrock first, then on Processing jobs. The Bedrock episode is the one to start from. It builds the whole WattBot pipeline, chunking the corpus included, from a cheap CPU notebook with nothing left running afterward. The Processing-jobs episode reruns the same pipeline on an open-weight model Bedrock does not carry, as jobs that end on their own, which shows what Bedrock does for you and what it costs to do yourself. An optional self-study episode runs the same self-hosted pipeline interactively on a GPU notebook instance, for the case where you need to work on a self-hosted model by hand, and only if you will remember to stop the instance. All three share one module of pipeline code, scripts/wattbot_rag.py in the lesson repository.

    When you build your own RAG system afterward, start from the Bedrock episode.

    Key Points
    • RAG is inference only. Nothing is trained or fine-tuned, so running one does not need a GPU of your own.
    • Bedrock is the default for inference: you pay per token, nothing runs between calls, and there is nothing to forget to shut down.
    • Self-managed GPU compute (Processing jobs, notebook GPUs, inference endpoints) is for a model Bedrock does not offer, or for batch volumes so large that per-token pricing loses; it is not a starting point.
    • Of the GPU options, Processing jobs are the safest, because the instance ends itself; notebook GPUs and endpoints bill by the hour until you stop them.
    • A forgotten GPU instance costs tens of dollars overnight and hundreds to thousands over a month; a full WattBot run on Bedrock costs under a dollar.
    • Tags never propagate. Tag every job at launch and route Bedrock calls through a tagged application inference profile, or the spend cannot be traced.
    • The hands-on episodes start with Bedrock, then the same pipeline on Processing jobs; the notebook-GPU version is optional self-study.

    Content from RAG with Bedrock

    Last updated on 2026-10-28 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 50 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do we build a complete RAG pipeline on AWS without provisioning a GPU?
    • How do we turn a collection of PDFs into retrievable, citable chunks stored in S3?
    • How do we call Bedrock-hosted embedding and generation models so that the spend is tagged to our project?

    Objectives

    • Read the WattBot metadata, questions and PDF corpus from the shared bucket, and cache what you derive from them (chunks.jsonl) in your own bucket for the later episodes.
    • Convert PDFs into page-level records and overlapping text chunks.
    • Create tagged application inference profiles so that every Bedrock call is attributed to your project.
    • Embed chunks with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings and retrieve relevant context with cosine similarity.
    • Generate WattBot-format answers and explanations with a Bedrock-hosted model (DeepSeek V3) and score them against train_QA.csv.
    • Build a second index from page images with a multimodal embedding model and measure what it changes for the table and figure questions.

    Open the notebook from: /ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/notebooks/11_RAG-Bedrock.ipynb. Select the conda_pytorch kernel. This is the first hands-on RAG episode, and it uses Amazon Bedrock, the default the overview recommended. We build the whole RAG pipeline for the WattBot 2026 challenge from a small CPU-only SageMaker notebook. Nothing here needs a GPU, because both the text embeddings and the answer generation run on Bedrock-hosted models, which bill per token and leave nothing running between calls. The two models are Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2, which turns WattBot chunks into vectors, and DeepSeek V3, which writes the answers and explanations.

    This episode also prepares the corpus. It unpacks the WattBot PDFs, splits them into pages and overlapping chunks, and caches the chunks in S3. The Processing-jobs episode and the optional GPU-notebook episode reuse those chunks and run the same retrieval, evaluation and scoring on self-hosted models, so cost, latency and effort can be compared directly.

    Why Bedrock for WattBot?

    With a self-hosted model, as in the Processing-jobs episode, you choose the model, keep its version, and make sure the instance has the GPU memory for it. That is fine for an experiment and a burden once several teams want the same pipeline. Running the embedding and generation steps on Bedrock means:

    • Managed models. Models from Anthropic, Amazon, DeepSeek and others, with no container images or CUDA versions of your own.
    • Paying per token. Instead of a GPU instance that may sit idle, you pay for the input and output tokens of each call. For most workloads that is cheaper; for a large offline batch with a small model, a GPU job can still win.
    • One set of models for a group. A lab or a course can agree on a few Bedrock models more easily than on a fleet of GPU instances.

    In this notebook both the embedding step and the answer and explanation steps run on Bedrock. The embeddings are saved as embeddings_bedrock.npy, so they can be compared with the self-hosted run in the Processing-jobs episode.

    Models used in this episode

    Both models are Bedrock-hosted foundation models:

    • Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 (amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0): a general text-embedding model for retrieval, clustering and classification. It returns vectors of 256, 512 or 1,024 dimensions, with presets for retrieval. AWS does not publish its parameter count.
    • DeepSeek V3 (deepseek.v3-v1:0): an open-weight mixture-of-experts model, 671B parameters in total and about 37B active per token, that Bedrock serves on demand, so there is no GPU to manage. Its per-token price is well below the flagship models’ (the Bedrock pricing page has current rates), which matters when there is one call per question. The same code works for any chat model in the catalog, because Bedrock’s one chat call, converse, takes the same input for every provider, a system prompt and a list of messages, and returns the reply in the same shape, so changing base_generation_model_id to a Claude, Llama or Mistral ID changes nothing else.
    • Multimodal models for tables and figures: Bedrock also serves models that embed or read images. Step 13 uses one, Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, on the table and figure questions.

    The model catalog in the Bedrock console lists every model available in the region (Claude variants, Amazon models and partner models), each with a model card and a link to its pricing.

    Callout

    Choosing the two models

    The catalog tells you what exists and what it costs; it does not tell you what is good. Three places do, and all three are free to read:

    • Embedding models: the MTEB leaderboard scores embedding models on retrieval benchmarks. Filter to the retrieval task and your language; the top of the table changes every few months, and Titan V2 is a sound middle-of-the-pack choice that Bedrock serves without setup.
    • Generation models: LMArena ranks chat models by blind human preference, and Artificial Analysis plots quality against price per million tokens, the chart to read for RAG, since the answer is written from retrieved text, so a mid-priced model often reads as well as a flagship at a tenth of the cost.
    • Your own questions: the benchmarks rank models on other people’s data. train_QA.csv has labelled questions for this corpus, and the evaluation at the end of this episode scores a model on them and prices the run from its token counts. Changing base_generation_model_id and rerunning is the whole experiment. A model that wins on a leaderboard and loses on your questions has told you something the leaderboard cannot.

    The habit is the same as for instances. Pick the cheapest candidate that scores well enough, measure it on your data, and move up only when the measurement says to.

    Notebook + dataset setup

    For this episode you need a SageMaker notebook instance, but not a GPU one. A small CPU instance such as ml.t3.medium is enough, because the models run on Bedrock, not in the notebook. The notebook’s execution role must allow Bedrock access, which a default SageMaker role does not. On the class account both roles the console offers carry it. On your own account, attach the Bedrock policy from the Account preparation checklist instructor page to your role before starting; the first Bedrock call fails with an access-denied error naming the role until it is there.

    See Instances for ML for further guidance on instance types.

    Two buckets, no uploads

    This episode reads from two buckets and you create neither of them here:

    • The shared bucket, ml-marathon-shared, already set in the setup cells below, holds the WattBot inputs under wattbot/: metadata.csv (the index of papers), train_QA.csv (labelled questions and answers), corpus.zip (the PDFs) and pages.jsonl (the text of every PDF page, extracted once). It is read-only and there is one copy for the whole class.
    • Your bucket from the S3 episode (challenge-lastnamefirstname) is where this episode writes what it derives, under a wattbot/ prefix: the chunked text (wattbot/chunks.jsonl), the embeddings (wattbot/embeddings/) and the predictions (wattbot/solutions/). Its tags cover its storage cost; your notebook instance carries the tags you gave it when you created it, and in this episode those two resources plus the per-token Bedrock calls (tagged through an inference profile, see “Cost tracking” below) are the only things being billed.
    Callout

    Working through the lesson on your own?

    If there is no instructor-staged bucket, stage the four input files in your own bucket under the same keys and point both variables at it: metadata.csv and train_QA.csv are in data/data.zip in the lesson repository, corpus.zip is built once by scripts/build_wattbot_corpus.py, and instructors/shared-data-bucket.md has the upload commands. Then set shared_bucket = bucket_name in the setup cell below and everything else works unchanged.

    Step 1 – Configure the notebook

    Three things are new here compared with the training episodes, so the setup is split into four cells.

    The session, region and S3 client are as before, plus the execution role, printed because the Bedrock calls below run as it.

    PYTHON 

    import os
import json
import time
from typing import Dict, Any, List
from pathlib import Path

import boto3
from botocore.config import Config
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "/home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts")   # the lesson's helper module, cloned in the controllers episode
import helpers
import sagemaker

session = sagemaker.Session()
region = session.boto_region_name
s3 = boto3.client("s3", region_name=region)
role = sagemaker.get_execution_role()
print("Role:", role)   # the execution role: on the class account it carries the Bedrock permissions; on your own, it must

    The models. RAG needs two, an embedding model, which turns a piece of text into a vector so that similar passages land near each other, and a generation model, the chat model that writes the answer from the passages it is given. Both are catalog models on Bedrock, named by a model ID; the model catalog in the console lists everything available in the region with its ID; prices are on the pricing page, and the supported models page in the documentation is the same list as a table. Prices are per million tokens on the Bedrock pricing page. In October 2026, DeepSeek V3 on demand is $0.62 in and $1.85 out, and Titan Text Embeddings V2 is $0.02 in, which is why the whole WattBot run below costs cents. We write the IDs down now but will not call them by these IDs directly, because the cost-tracking step below wraps each one in a tagged inference profile first, because that is the only way Bedrock spend gets attributed to a project.

    PYTHON 

    # Base model IDs. Any chat model in the Bedrock catalog works as the generator (a Claude or Llama ID, say),
# because converse, Bedrock's chat call, takes the same messages and returns the same shape for every provider.
base_generation_model_id = "deepseek.v3-v1:0"             # writes the answers; $0.62 in / $1.85 out per million tokens (Oct 2026)
base_embedding_model_id = "amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0"  # turns text into vectors for retrieval; $0.02 per million tokens

    The files. The inputs in the shared bucket are the paper list, the questions with their answers, and the zipped corpus of PDFs. Everything this episode derives from them goes to your own bucket, under the same wattbot/ prefix, which will hold the chunked text, the chunk embeddings, and the answers the pipeline produces.

    PYTHON 

    !mkdir -p /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/wattbot   # a project folder beside the lesson clone, so data and outputs stay out of the repository
%cd /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/wattbot

shared_bucket = "ml-marathon-shared"   # the instructor-staged, read-only bucket with the data and model weights; change only on your own account
bucket_name = "sinkorswim-doejohn"     # <-- EDIT ME: your own bucket from the S3 episode

# inputs, in the shared bucket
metadata_key = "wattbot/metadata.csv"      # one row per paper: id, title, url
train_key = "wattbot/train_QA.csv"         # the questions, with reference answers for scoring
corpus_key = "wattbot/corpus.zip"          # the PDFs, one per paper

# derived, written to YOUR bucket
chunks_key = "wattbot/chunks.jsonl"                                # the corpus cut into passages (end of the chunking step)
embeddings_key = "wattbot/embeddings/embeddings_bedrock.npy"       # one vector per chunk
solutions_key = "wattbot/solutions/wattbot_solutions_bedrock.csv"  # the pipeline's answers, in the competition's format

local_data_dir = "./data"              # working copies on this notebook instance
os.makedirs(local_data_dir, exist_ok=True)

    The inputs, as they sit in the shared bucket. The three files named above are at the top of wattbot/; the rest of the folder is what the instructor staged for the caching steps later in the episode.

    PYTHON 

    helpers.show_bucket(shared_bucket, "wattbot/")   # every file under the prefix, with its size

    Two Bedrock clients. Bedrock has two APIs. bedrock-runtime is the one that calls models (converse, the chat call, for answers; invoke_model, the raw call with a provider-specific body, for embeddings); it is what every answer and every embedding in this episode goes through. bedrock is the control plane, for listing models and creating the inference profiles that carry our tags. The runtime client gets a retry setting because on-demand Bedrock throughput is rate-limited per model, so a loop of a few thousand embedding calls will occasionally be throttled, and the adaptive mode backs off and retries instead of raising.

    PYTHON 

    bedrock_runtime = boto3.client(
    "bedrock-runtime",
    region_name=region,
    config=Config(retries={"max_attempts": 10, "mode": "adaptive"}),   # back off and retry when throttled
)
bedrock = boto3.client("bedrock", region_name=region)                  # control plane: list models, create inference profiles

    Step 2 – Get the shared WattBot helpers

    The retrieval, prompting, answer parsing and scoring logic of the WattBot pipeline is the same whether the models run on Bedrock, in a Processing job or on a notebook GPU. It lives once in the lesson repository, in scripts/wattbot_rag.py, and every RAG episode imports it; the only code that differs per episode is the two model calls. Copy the module from the lesson clone to the folder next to this notebook (the Processing Jobs episode ships the same file inside its jobs).

    PYTHON

    ANSWER_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
