    Read the per-type lines against the DeepSeek run. A cheaper model that holds its own on Quote questions and loses on Math and CrossPaper is the usual pattern; whether that trade is worth it depends on which questions you have.

    Embedder. First list the embedding models the region’s catalog has, because model IDs come and go and an ID that is not in the list fails at the profile step with “The provided model identifier is invalid”:

    PYTHON 

    for m in bedrock.list_foundation_models(byOutputModality="EMBEDDING")["modelSummaries"]:
    print(f"{m['modelId']:<45} {m['providerName']}")

    Cohere’s request takes a list of texts and says whether they are documents or a query; its response is a list of vectors, nested under the number type asked for. One wrinkle. The catalog lists cohere.embed-v4:0 for Ohio, but creating a profile on it fails with “does not support On Demand inference”, because in this region the model is served only through the US cross-region profile, us.cohere.embed-v4:0. tagged_profile_arn catches that error and switches to the us. ID itself, which is the same thing that happens for Llama 4 and several other models. Everything else is Step 8 again, a tagged profile, one call per chunk, a cached matrix, and a query function that uses the same model.

    PYTHON 

    %%script false --no-raise-error
# Challenge solution: delete the line above to run this cell. Ten minutes of embedding, so not in class.
cohere_model_id = "cohere.embed-v4:0"   # listed for Ohio but served only through the US cross-region profile; tagged_profile_arn switches to us.cohere.embed-v4:0 on its own
cohere_arn = tagged_profile_arn(bedrock, cohere_model_id, "wattbot-embed-cohere", name, project)

def cohere_embed(text: str, input_type: str = "search_document") -> np.ndarray:
    """One Cohere Embed v4 vector; input_type is search_document for the corpus, search_query for a question."""
    body = {"texts": [text[:2000]], "input_type": input_type, "embedding_types": ["float"]}
    response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model(modelId=cohere_arn, contentType="application/json", accept="application/json", body=json.dumps(body))
    return np.asarray(json.loads(response["body"].read())["embeddings"]["float"][0], dtype="float32")

cohere_emb_path = data_dir / "embeddings_cohere.npy"   # a new file: the Titan matrix stays
if cohere_emb_path.exists():
    cohere_embeddings = np.load(cohere_emb_path)
else:
    t0 = time.time()
    cohere_embeddings = np.vstack([cohere_embed(ch["text"]) for ch in chunked_docs])
    np.save(cohere_emb_path, cohere_embeddings)
    print(f"Embedded {len(chunked_docs)} chunks in {(time.time() - t0) / 60:.1f} min")

def embed_query_cohere(question: str) -> np.ndarray:
    return cohere_embed(question, input_type="search_query")

    Then the Step 11 loop with embed_query=embed_query_cohere and chunk_embeddings=cohere_embeddings, DeepSeek unchanged, and the scorer. The hit-rate cell from Step 13 is the sharper instrument here. Compute it for the new matrix before scoring, because an embedder that finds the paper less often cannot be rescued by any generator. A cheaper variant of the same experiment keeps Titan and adds "dimensions": 256 to its request body in Step 8, which asks whether a four-times smaller index retrieves as well.

    Step 13 – Multimodal embeddings for the table and figure questions

    Look back at the evidence-type table in Step 12. The Table and Figure rows are usually the worst, and the reason is upstream of the model. pypdf gives us a page’s text, so a table comes out as a run of numbers with its column headers somewhere else on the page, and a figure comes out as its caption and nothing more. A question whose answer is a bar in a plot has nothing in the chunks to find, and a question whose answer is a cell in a table is being read from a flattened copy.

    A multimodal embedding model is one model that maps text and images into the same vector space, so a text question can be compared with an image directly, and the picture of a table lands near a sentence about its contents. Bedrock has two from Amazon, Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings (text, images, documents, video and audio, released 2025) and the older Titan Multimodal Embeddings G1 (text and images). Both are per-call, like Titan Text, and billed per image plus per text token; the Bedrock pricing page has the rates, on the order of a hundredth of a cent per image. One catch. In October 2026 Nova Multimodal Embeddings is offered in us-east-1 and not in Ohio (check the model catalog for that region). A Bedrock call is an HTTPS request and the region is a parameter, so from Ohio that is a second client pointed at Virginia; it also means the images leave the region, which is the thing to check against your institution’s data policy before doing this with documents that are not public papers.

    This step cuts the tables and figures out of the PDFs as images, builds a second index from them next to the text one, measures whether it finds the right paper for table and figure questions more often, and then hands the images to a model that can look at them. Each cell is short because the plumbing is in wattbot_rag.py.

    Extract the tables and figures

    Why cut them out at all, instead of handing the embedding model a whole page, or the PDF itself (Nova accepts documents as input)? For the same reason Step 6 cut the text into chunks instead of embedding each paper whole. An embedding is a fixed-length vector, a thousand numbers, whatever goes in; the more that goes in, the less of each thing survives in it. A page holding two tables, a figure and three paragraphs gets one vector that is a blur of all six, and a question about one of the tables has to match that blur. A crop of the table gets a vector that is about the table. The same holds at generation time. The vision model reads a crop at full resolution for a few hundred tokens, where a page costs a thousand tokens and shows the table at a quarter of the size. We tried whole pages first on this corpus. They helped figure questions a little and tables not at all. The crops, as the callout at the end shows, help both.

    A PDF has no table or figure objects to pull out. It stores text runs, raster images, and drawing commands (lines, fills, curves), and a plot is a few thousand of the last. PyMuPDF ships three detectors that turn those back into boxes. find_tables finds tables from their rulings or their text alignment, get_image_info lists the embedded raster images, and cluster_drawings groups the drawing commands of a vector figure into one bounding box. extract_figures_and_tables in wattbot_rag.py runs the three on every page, drops page-sized background fills, rules and logos, pairs each box with the nearest caption line starting “Table N” or “Figure N” (tables are captioned above, figures below) and widens the crop to include that caption, so the image carries the identifier a question will use. A caption whose box no detector found falls back to the whole page, so nothing the text mentions is missed. Open the function; it is about eighty lines, and every rule in it is a line you can change. The detectors are the slow part, a second or two per page on this instance, so the cell runs them only on the pages whose text carries a caption, under half of the corpus; in class, with use_instructor_embeddings set, it downloads the crops your instructor made instead.

    PYTHON 

    %pip install -q pymupdf

    PYTHON 

    from wattbot_rag import extract_figures_and_tables, find_caption_pages, embed_multimodal, image_blocks, hit_at_k

crop_dir = data_dir / "crops"
crops_path = data_dir / "crops.jsonl"
shared_crops_key = "wattbot/crops.zip"   # the instructor's crops, staged like the embeddings

if not crops_path.exists() and use_instructor_embeddings and _s3_object_exists(shared_bucket, shared_crops_key):
    s3.download_file(shared_bucket, shared_crops_key, str(data_dir / "crops.zip"))
    with zipfile.ZipFile(data_dir / "crops.zip") as zf:
        zf.extractall(data_dir)
    (data_dir / "crops.zip").unlink()
    print("Downloaded the instructor's crops")

if crops_path.exists():
    crops = [json.loads(line) for line in open(crops_path)]
else:
    caption_pages: Dict[str, Dict[int, set]] = {}   # per paper, the pages whose text carries a caption, and which kinds: the detectors run only there
    for p in find_caption_pages(page_docs):
        caption_pages.setdefault(p["doc_id"], {})[p["page_num"]] = {"table" if c.startswith("Table") else "figure" for c in p["captions"]}
    t0 = time.time()
    crops = []
    for i, (doc_id, page_nums) in enumerate(sorted(caption_pages.items())):
        crops += extract_figures_and_tables(os.path.join(PDF_DIR, f"{doc_id}.pdf"), doc_id, crop_dir, pages=page_nums)
        if (i + 1) % 10 == 0:
            print(f"{i + 1} papers, {len(crops)} crops so far ({time.time() - t0:.0f} s)")
    with open(crops_path, "w") as f:
        f.writelines(json.dumps(c) + "\n" for c in crops)
    print(f"Extracted {len(crops)} crops from {len(caption_pages)} papers in {(time.time() - t0) / 60:.1f} min")

n_tables = sum(c["kind"] == "table" for c in crops)
n_pages = sum(c["whole_page"] for c in crops)
print(f"{n_tables} tables and {len(crops) - n_tables} figures; {n_pages} of them are whole-page fallbacks")
crops[:3]

    Look at a few before trusting them. A crop that is a logo, a page rule, or half a plot tells you which threshold to change.

    PYTHON 

    from IPython.display import Image, display

for c in [c for c in crops if c["kind"] == "table"][:2] + [c for c in crops if c["kind"] == "figure"][:2]:
    print(f"{c['doc_id']} page {c['page_label']}: {c['caption']}")
    display(Image(filename=c["png_path"], width=500))

    Embed the crops

    The embedding model lives in us-east-1, so this is a second runtime client pointed there. One difference from the text models is that Bedrock rejects this model’s request body when it arrives through an application inference profile, so these calls use the model ID directly and are the one Bedrock spend in this lesson that carries no project tags. embed_multimodal builds the model’s request body (Nova’s says whether a vector is for the index or for a query, and that the image is a document, not a photo) and returns a unit vector. Set multimodal_model_id to amazon.titan-embed-image-v1 to try the older model; the function handles both.

    PYTHON 

    multimodal_region = "us-east-1"
multimodal_model_id = "amazon.nova-2-multimodal-embeddings-v1:0"   # called by ID: this model does not accept calls through an inference profile

bedrock_runtime_mm = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name=multimodal_region,
                                  config=Config(retries={"max_attempts": 10, "mode": "adaptive"}))

v = embed_multimodal(bedrock_runtime_mm, multimodal_model_id, image_png=Path(crops[0]["png_path"]).read_bytes())
print(f"{crops[0]['doc_id']} {crops[0]['caption'][:40]!r} -> vector of {v.shape[0]} dimensions")

    One call per crop, cached like the text matrix, locally, then in your bucket, then computed. The loop runs six calls at a time through a thread pool and prints every fifty; the 2,213 crops take about four minutes. The question side uses the same model with purpose="query".

    PYTHON 

    crop_emb_path = data_dir / "embeddings_crops_multimodal.npy"
crop_emb_key = "wattbot/embeddings/embeddings_crops_multimodal.npy"

if crop_emb_path.exists():
    crop_embeddings = np.load(crop_emb_path)
elif use_instructor_embeddings and _s3_object_exists(shared_bucket, "wattbot/embeddings_crops_multimodal.npy"):
    s3.download_file(shared_bucket, "wattbot/embeddings_crops_multimodal.npy", str(crop_emb_path))
    crop_embeddings = np.load(crop_emb_path)
    print("Downloaded the instructor's crop embeddings")
elif _s3_object_exists(bucket_name, crop_emb_key):
    s3.download_file(bucket_name, crop_emb_key, str(crop_emb_path))
    crop_embeddings = np.load(crop_emb_path)
else:
    from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

    def embed_crop(c):
        return embed_multimodal(bedrock_runtime_mm, multimodal_model_id, image_png=Path(c["png_path"]).read_bytes())

    t0 = time.time()
    rows = []
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=6) as pool:   # one image per call: six in flight at a time
        for i, vec in enumerate(pool.map(embed_crop, crops)):
            rows.append(vec)
            if (i + 1) % 50 == 0:
                print(f"Embedded {i + 1} / {len(crops)} crops ({time.time() - t0:.0f} s, {(i + 1) / (time.time() - t0):.1f} per second)")
    crop_embeddings = np.vstack(rows)
    np.save(crop_emb_path, crop_embeddings)
    s3.upload_file(str(crop_emb_path), bucket_name, crop_emb_key)
    print(f"Embedded {len(crops)} crops in {(time.time() - t0) / 60:.1f} min")

assert crop_embeddings.shape[0] == len(crops), "crop embeddings and crops are out of step; delete the cached file and rerun"
print("Crop embeddings shape:", crop_embeddings.shape)

def embed_query_mm(question: str) -> np.ndarray:
    return embed_multimodal(bedrock_runtime_mm, multimodal_model_id, text=question, purpose="query")

    Does the image index find the right table or figure?

    Retrieval is the same retrieve_top_k as Step 9, over the crop matrix instead of the chunk matrix. Two measures, both hit rates, higher is better, 1.00 meaning every question had it. The first is coarse. Is a ground-truth paper among the top results? train_QA.csv names the paper for every question. The second is the one that matters for this step. Is the table or figure the answer sits in among the crops the model would be shown? Most table and figure questions name it in supporting_materials (“Table 3”, “Fig. 5, upper panel”), and cited_captions pulls that identifier out; crop_matches checks a crop’s caption against it. For the text index, the crops it “shows” are those on the pages its top chunks came from, which is what the third vision run below attaches. Quote-only questions are the control for the paper measure, where the image index should have no advantage.

    PYTHON 

    from wattbot_rag import cited_captions, crop_matches

k = 8
groups = {"Table": train_df[train_df["Table"] == 1], "Figure": train_df[train_df["Figure"] == 1],
          "Quote only": train_df[(train_df["Quote"] == 1) & (train_df["Table"] == 0) & (train_df["Figure"] == 0)].head(40)}
crops_by_page: Dict[tuple, list] = {}
for c in crops:
    crops_by_page.setdefault((c["doc_id"], c["page_num"]), []).append(c)

def crops_behind(chunks):   # the crops on the pages the retrieved chunks came from
    return [c for ch in chunks for c in crops_by_page.get((ch["doc_id"], ch["page_num"]), [])]

print("Hit rate (higher is better). Paper: a ground-truth paper is in the top 8 results. Table/figure: the one the answer")
print("sits in is among the crops shown (the image index's top 3; for the text index, the crops on its top chunks' pages)\n")
print(f"{'questions':<12}{'n':>4}{'paper, text':>14}{'paper, image':>14}{'crop, text':>14}{'crop, image':>14}")
for label, qs in groups.items():
    gt = [split_ref_ids(r) for r in qs["ref_id"]]
    text_chunks = [retrieve_top_k(embed_query(q), chunk_embeddings, chunked_docs, k=k) for q in qs["question"]]
    image_crops = [retrieve_top_k(embed_query_mm(q), crop_embeddings, crops, k=3) for q in qs["question"]]
    paper_text = hit_at_k([[c["doc_id"] for c in r] for r in text_chunks], gt)
    paper_image = hit_at_k([[c["doc_id"] for c in r] for r in image_crops], gt)
    # the crop measure, over the questions that name their table or figure
    targets = [(refs, cited_captions(sm)) for refs, sm in zip(gt, qs["supporting_materials"])]
    crop_text, crop_image, n_named = [], [], 0
    for (refs, labels), chunks_i, crops_i in zip(targets, text_chunks, image_crops):
        if not labels:
            continue
        n_named += 1
        crop_text.append(any(crop_matches(c, d, l) for c in crops_behind(chunks_i) for d in refs for l in labels))
        crop_image.append(any(crop_matches(c, d, l) for c in crops_i for d in refs for l in labels))
    crop_cols = f"{np.mean(crop_text):>14.2f}{np.mean(crop_image):>14.2f}  (of {n_named} that name one)" if n_named else f"{'':>14}{'':>14}"
    print(f"{label:<12}{len(qs):>4}{paper_text:>14.2f}{paper_image:>14.2f}{crop_cols}")

    Read the paper columns first. Both indexes find the paper for nearly every table and figure question, so at that level there is nothing to win, and the image index is behind. The crop columns are the real comparison. They say whether the text route, chunks and the crops on their pages, or the image route, the crops themselves, more often puts the exact table or figure in front of the model. If the image column is higher there while the paper column is lower, the image index is doing a different job than the text index, finding the object, not the document, and the next cells show whether the model can use it. If both crop columns are low, the fix is upstream, in the extraction, where a table the detector missed became a whole-page fallback, and a page is a weak key.

    Let the model see the table or figure

    Finding the table is half of it; DeepSeek V3 reads text only, so a figure retrieved as an image is no use to it. converse accepts image blocks in a user message for models that can see, and the swap is the model ID. Amazon Nova 2 Lite reads images and documents and is in the catalog for Ohio through the cross-region profile below (check the model catalog; us.amazon.nova-lite-v1:0 is the cheaper, weaker alternative). call_vision_chat is call_bedrock_chat with an images argument. For each attached crop it adds a text label naming the paper and the caption, then the image, so the model can cite what it reads.

    PYTHON 

    base_vision_model_id = "us.amazon.nova-2-lite-v1:0"
vision_model_id = tagged_profile_arn(bedrock, base_vision_model_id, "wattbot-vision", name, project)
vision_usage = []

def call_vision_chat(system_prompt: str, user_prompt: str, max_new_tokens: int = 512, images=()) -> str:
    """One system + user turn, with zero or more (label, png_bytes) images attached to the user turn."""
    content = [{"text": user_prompt}]
    if images:
        content.append({"text": "The images below are tables and figures from the same papers; read values from them where the text above is incomplete."})
        content.extend(image_blocks(images))
    response = bedrock_runtime.converse(
        modelId=vision_model_id,
        system=[{"text": system_prompt}],
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": content}],
        inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": max_new_tokens, "temperature": 0},
    )
    vision_usage.append(response["usage"])
    return "\n".join(b["text"] for b in response["output"]["message"]["content"] if "text" in b).strip()

def crop_label(c) -> str:
    return f"{c['doc_id']}, page {c['page_label']}, {c['caption'][:60]}" if c["caption"] else f"{c['doc_id']}, page {c['page_label']}"

print(call_vision_chat("You are a concise assistant.", "What is in the attached image? One sentence.", 64,
                       images=[(crop_label(crops[0]), Path(crops[0]["png_path"]).read_bytes())]))

    Three runs over the Table and Figure questions, all through the vision model, so that the only thing changing between them is what the model is shown. The first is the control, text chunks only. The second attaches the top three crops from the image index. The third attaches the crops from the pages the top text chunks came from. If the hit-rate table says the text index is the better finder, the question is whether finding with text and reading with the image is the better split. Each run is the same loop as Step 11, so every question costs an answer call and an explanation call; our runs took 1.6, 4.0 and 3.0 minutes, the image runs longer because every attached crop is hundreds of input tokens. In class, with use_instructor_embeddings set, the cell downloads the three result files from your instructor’s run of it instead and the next cell scores them; running the loops yourself is for after class.

    PYTHON 

    tf_df = train_df[(train_df["Table"] == 1) | (train_df["Figure"] == 1)]
print(f"{len(tf_df)} table and figure questions; each run makes an answer call and an explanation call per question, so about {6 * len(tf_df)} calls for three runs")

def crops_for(question: str, images_from: str):
    """The crops to attach: none, the image index's top three, or those on the pages behind the top text chunks."""
    if images_from == "image_index":
        return retrieve_top_k(embed_query_mm(question), crop_embeddings, crops, k=3)
    if images_from == "text_index":
        found = []
        for c in crops_behind(retrieve_top_k(embed_query(question), chunk_embeddings, chunked_docs, k=8)):
            if c not in found:
                found.append(c)
        return found[:3]
    return []

def run_tf(images_from: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    rows = []
    for i, (_, row) in enumerate(tf_df.iterrows(), start=1):
        images = [(crop_label(c), Path(c["png_path"]).read_bytes()) for c in crops_for(row["question"], images_from)]
        generate = lambda s, u, max_new_tokens=512, images=images: call_vision_chat(s, u, max_new_tokens, images=images)
        rows.append(run_single_qa(row=row, embed_query=embed_query, generate=generate, chunk_embeddings=chunk_embeddings,
                                  chunked_docs=chunked_docs, docid_to_url=docid_to_url, top_k=8, retrieval_threshold=0.25))
        if i % 10 == 0:
            print(f"  {i} / {len(tf_df)} questions ({time.time() - t0:.0f} s)")
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

vision_runs = {"text chunks only": "none", "chunks + crops from the image index": "image_index", "chunks + crops behind the text chunks": "text_index"}
vision_files = {images_from: f"wattbot_solutions_vision_{images_from}.csv" for images_from in vision_runs.values()}

t0 = time.time()
for label, images_from in vision_runs.items():
    local_path = os.path.join(output_dir, vision_files[images_from])
    shared_key = f"wattbot/solutions/{vision_files[images_from]}"
    if use_instructor_embeddings and _s3_object_exists(shared_bucket, shared_key):   # in class: the instructor's run of this cell, scored in the next
        s3.download_file(shared_bucket, shared_key, local_path)
        print(f"{label}: downloaded the instructor's results")
        continue
    print(f"{label}: running")
    run_tf(images_from).to_csv(local_path, index=False)
    s3.upload_file(local_path, bucket_name, shared_key)   # kept in your bucket too, next to the Step 11 predictions
    print(f"{label}: done at {(time.time() - t0) / 60:.1f} min")

    Score all three the same way as Step 12. The scorer compares the rows it finds, so the breakdown is over these questions only; the Table and Figure lines are the ones to read, across the three runs and against the DeepSeek run.

    PYTHON 

    for label, images_from in vision_runs.items():
    print("=" * 96)
    print(f"Nova 2 Lite, {label}")
    compute_wattbot_score(train_qa_path=train_qa_path, preds_path=os.path.join(output_dir, f"wattbot_solutions_vision_{images_from}.csv"), n_examples=3)
    Callout

    What to expect, and what it cost

    Measured once on this corpus, 50 table and figure questions, Nova 2 Lite throughout. At the paper level the text index wins. A ground-truth paper is in its top 8 for 94% of table questions and 94% of figure questions, against 77% and 71% for the image index, and for 82% against 55% of quote-only questions, where a picture has nothing to offer. At the crop level the two routes are even. The crop the answer sits in is among those shown for 55% of table questions by the text route and 52% by the image index, and for 57% against 50% of figure questions. Then reading. Text chunks alone scored 0.64, with 57% of table answers and 59% of figure answers correct. Chunks plus the image index’s top three crops scored 0.75, with 69% of tables and 71% of figures correct and citation F1 up from 0.85 to 0.93. Chunks plus the crops on the pages behind the top text chunks, the route the paper-level hit rate seemed to favour, scored 0.67. Two readings. Showing the model the table or figure is worth about ten points on the questions that depend on one, tables included, which whole pages at 100 dpi had not managed. And the crop-level hit rates say where the image index’s lead does not come from. It finds the answer’s own crop no more often than the text route does. The difference is in what else the model is shown, three crops chosen by their similarity to the question against every crop on the pages behind the top chunks. Fifty questions is a small sample, so read the direction, not the decimals. For the bill, every crop is a few hundred input tokens at Nova 2 Lite’s rate on the pricing page, so a run with images costs two to three times the control and takes three to four times as long, 1.6, 4.0 and 3.0 minutes for the three runs here. vision_usage holds all three runs’ usage blocks, and the embedding of the 2,213 crops is the per-image rate times that count, a few cents.

    Wrap-up

    You now have a complete WattBot evaluation on Bedrock, billed per token, with nothing left running. The Processing-jobs episode reruns it on a self-hosted model, and the optional GPU-notebook episode once more by hand, so by the end there are three versions of the same pipeline to compare, Bedrock, a Processing job and a notebook GPU. The code they share is the retrieval, prompting and scoring in wattbot_rag.py; what each one implements is the two callables, embed_query and generate.

    Use Bedrock or another hosted API when a catalog model will do, when the number of questions is modest or you are still prototyping, and when you would rather pay per token than manage a GPU. Use a self-hosted model on a GPU when the work needs a model the catalog does not carry, when you will run large batches repeatedly, when you need control over the exact checkpoint, or when you already have GPUs you are not paying for by the hour.

    The model is one part of a RAG system, and not the part where most of the accuracy is won. A bigger or newer model does not fix weak retrieval. If the chunks do not match the questions, a strong model still has nothing to read. The gains over time come from the work around the model, chunking, metadata and filtering, reranking, post-processing, and the score breakdown by evidence type in Step 12 says which of them to work on. A bigger model or a longer prompt raises the bill per question as well as the score, and Bedrock lets you measure that trade by changing one model ID.

    Key Points
    • A complete RAG pipeline on AWS needs no GPU. A CPU notebook plus Bedrock-hosted embedding and generation models is enough.
    • Corpus preparation (unpacking the staged PDFs, page extraction, chunking) is cheap CPU work; cache chunks.jsonl on S3 so later episodes and runs can reuse it.
    • Bedrock calls carry no tags; route them through a tagged application inference profile or the spend is anonymous on the bill.
    • converse is the provider-neutral way to call a chat model on Bedrock; its usage block is what you are billed on. DeepSeek V3 is the generator here, and any catalog model is a one-line swap.
    • Bedrock bills per token and leaves nothing running between calls, which is why it is the default route for RAG inference.
    • The model is one tunable component; most accuracy gains come from chunking, retrieval, and post-processing.

    Content from RAG with Processing Jobs

    Last updated on 2026-10-28 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 50 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • When does a RAG pipeline need a self-hosted, open-weight model instead of Bedrock?
    • How do we run the embedding and generation steps of the WattBot pipeline as SageMaker Processing jobs that end on their own?
    • How do we pass data in and out of a job through S3, and tag the job so its cost is traceable?

    Objectives

    • Explain why Bedrock’s catalog is not enough when you need a specific open-weight model, and why a Processing job is the default way to self-host one for batch work.
    • Launch a GPU Processing job that embeds the cached WattBot chunks with a self-hosted embedding model and writes the vectors to S3.
    • Launch a second Processing job that runs Qwen3-8B (an open-weight model in a size Bedrock does not carry) with transformers and runs the full RAG loop over the training questions.
    • Read a job’s inputs, outputs, arguments and runtime cap, and relate its duration to what it cost.
    • Score the batch predictions with the WattBot metric and compare against the Bedrock run.

    Open the notebook from: /ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/notebooks/12_RAG-Processing-jobs.ipynb. Select the conda_pytorch kernel.

    When Bedrock does not have your model

    The Bedrock episode built the whole WattBot pipeline without managing a GPU, and that stays the simplest choice whenever Bedrock carries a model that will do. Research often depends on a particular open-weight checkpoint, though. A newly released model, a smaller size, a fine-tune for scientific text, a model a paper just published. Bedrock’s catalog is curated. It carries Amazon’s models, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek and a few others, and within a family only some sizes, usually a generation behind. For Qwen, the serverless lineup is still the Qwen3 series. Hugging Face hosts well over a million open-weight checkpoints, and the one you want is usually not on Bedrock, and often never will be.

    In that case you run the model on hardware you rent through SageMaker, and the next decision is how long to keep that hardware. SageMaker rents a GPU three ways.

    Bills Stops when Best for
    GPU notebook instance by the hour from start to stop you stop it interactive debugging, prototyping at the keyboard
    Processing or training job by the second while the job runs the script ends, or max_runtime_in_seconds batch work: embed a corpus, answer a list of questions, train
    Inference endpoint by the hour while deployed you delete it serving a model to an application with steady traffic

    For research RAG, almost all the work is batch. Embed everything once, answer a list of questions, score them. That is a job, and a job is the one option that releases the instance on its own, so it cannot be forgotten. This episode runs the WattBot pipeline as two jobs. The first turns the cached chunks into embeddings with thenlper/gte-large. The second loads the generator, retrieves evidence for each question and writes answers in WattBot’s submission format. The notebook stays a small CPU instance that never touches a model. It stages data, launches the jobs and reads the results back.

    The generator is Qwen3-8B, an 8-billion-parameter open-weight model (Apache 2.0). Bedrock serves the 32B and 235B members of that family but not this size, which is the usual situation, where the size you want is the one missing. The job runs it with transformers, the same library the fine-tuning episode trained with. from_pretrained downloads the weights onto the GPU, and generate writes the answer to a chat prompt, the self-hosted counterpart of what Bedrock does behind converse. Inference needs no gradients, so the weights are the memory cost, and 8B parameters at two bytes each in bf16 is about 16 GB, which fits the 24 GB GPU of an ml.g5.xlarge with room for the KV cache. (The fine-tuning episode has the full memory arithmetic; the short version is that inference needs only the weights and training needs eight times more per parameter.)

    Open-weight models that fit one GPU are now close to the frontier on the kinds of tasks research code runs, on data that never leaves your account. The newest of this family, Qwen3.8-27B, fits one GPU and lands within a few points of a frontier commercial model:

    Qwen figures are from the Qwen3.8-27B model card and were not reproduced here; Opus 4.8 figures are from its published evaluations.

    Callout

    What this episode costs

    Rates are us-east-1 on-demand from the Instances for ML page.

    Job Instance $/h Expected duration Cost
    Embed ~9,000 chunks ml.g5.xlarge (A10G, 24 GB) $1.41 ~10 min incl. startup ~$0.20
    RAG over a 53-question sample with Qwen3-8B ml.g5.xlarge (A10G, 24 GB) $1.41 ~15 min: 1 provisioning, ~8 downloading and loading 16 GB of weights, ~6 generating ~$0.35
    Controller notebook ml.t3.medium $0.05 2 h $0.10

    About $0.65 for the episode, and the GPUs are off the moment each script ends. The RAG job answers the same stratified sample of questions as the Bedrock episode (ten per evidence type, 53 questions once the two papers the corpus lacks are dropped); all 220 is about an hour of generation, so run that at home. Both jobs carry max_runtime_in_seconds, so a hung job costs at most the cap. Compare the same pipeline on a GPU notebook instance (the optional GPU-notebook episode that follows), where the meter runs until someone stops it, and a forgotten ml.g5.xlarge is $34 a day.

    The trade-off is latency. A job takes minutes to start, so this pattern is for batch questions, not a chatbot. For interactive use, Bedrock answers in seconds; for interactive use of a model Bedrock does not have, an inference endpoint does, at an hourly rate you have to remember to turn off.

    In this episode we will:

    • Reuse the chunks cached in your bucket by the Bedrock episode and the inputs in the shared bucket.
    • Run two short-lived GPU Processing jobs. One computes embeddings for all chunks, the second runs Qwen3-8B with transformers and the full RAG loop (retrieval + generation) over the same 53-question sample as the Bedrock episode.
    • Score the result and compare it with the Bedrock run. The retrieval logic, prompts and scorer are unchanged, so the comparison is of the models, not of the pipeline.

    Setup

    A code folder for each job

    A Processing job runs in a container on a separate machine. It cannot see the Python variables or files that exist only in this notebook, and the only code it gets is the one directory named by source_dir=, uploaded whole, the same way the training estimator’s source_dir worked in the fine-tuning episode. The four scripts the jobs need are already on this instance, in the lesson clone, but pointing source_dir at the lesson’s whole scripts/ directory would upload every script in the workshop. So each job gets a small folder holding just the files it imports, copied out of the clone. The four files:

    • scripts/embedding_inference.py: generic embedding script (JSONL with a text field in, embeddings.npy out).
    • scripts/hf_embedder.py: the embedding model wrapper both jobs use, on plain transformers (mean pooling and normalisation, thirty lines), so neither job has to install anything for it.
    • scripts/wattbot_rag_batch.py: the WattBot RAG loop as a batch job: loads the inputs, runs the generator, writes wattbot_solutions.csv.
    • scripts/wattbot_rag.py: the shared pipeline logic (retrieval, prompts, answer parsing, run_single_qa, the scorer) that the Bedrock episode imported too. The batch script imports it, so it ships with the job; the notebook imports it for scoring.

    The cell below copies them into the project folder, code_embed/ for the embedding job and code_rag/ for the RAG job. The copies of wattbot_rag.py and Score.py next to the notebook are for the scoring step at the end, which runs in the notebook, not in a job.

    PYTHON 

    !mkdir -p /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/wattbot   # the same project folder the Bedrock episode used, beside the lesson clone
%cd /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/wattbot

# One source directory per job: SageMaker uploads the whole directory into the container
!mkdir -p code_embed code_rag
# The embedding job's script
!cp /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/embedding_inference.py /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/hf_embedder.py code_embed/
# The RAG job's script plus the shared module it imports (the container cannot see this notebook)
!cp /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/wattbot_rag_batch.py /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/wattbot_rag.py /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/hf_embedder.py code_rag/
# The notebook's own copies, for scoring at the end: the pipeline module and the competition's metric file
!cp /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/wattbot_rag.py /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/Score.py .
!ls code_embed code_rag

    Now connect the notebook to SageMaker and S3. The shared bucket holds the challenge data. Your own bucket holds the chunks the Bedrock episode cached and will receive the job outputs.

    PYTHON 

    import os
import json

import boto3
import time
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import sagemaker
from sagemaker import get_execution_role
from sagemaker.huggingface import HuggingFaceProcessor         # launches a job in the prebuilt Hugging Face container
from sagemaker.processing import ProcessingInput, ProcessingOutput   # S3 <-> container path mappings for a job

session = sagemaker.Session()
region = session.boto_region_name
role = get_execution_role()   # the IAM role the jobs run under to read and write S3

shared_bucket = "ml-marathon-shared"   # the instructor-staged, read-only bucket with the data and model weights; change only on your own account
bucket_name = "sinkorswim-doejohn"     # <-- EDIT ME: your own bucket (chunks in, outputs out)
s3_client = boto3.client("s3", region_name=region)

local_data_dir = "./data"
os.makedirs(local_data_dir, exist_ok=True)

print("Region:", region)
print("Role:", role)
print("Bucket:", bucket_name)

    Step 1 – Check the inputs

    The jobs read three files from S3, train_QA.csv and metadata.csv from the shared bucket, and chunks.jsonl from your bucket, where the Bedrock episode cached it. The PDFs themselves are not needed again, because chunking was done once, and the jobs work from the chunks. We download the three files to the notebook only to confirm they exist and to look at them; the jobs fetch their own copies from S3.

    First the keys and the full S3 URIs. The URIs are the form a ProcessingInput takes, so they are built here once and reused when the jobs are launched.

    PYTHON 

    train_qa_key = "wattbot/train_QA.csv"
metadata_key = "wattbot/metadata.csv"
chunks_s3_key = "wattbot/chunks.jsonl"

# Full S3 URIs: this is the form a ProcessingInput takes
train_qa_s3 = f"s3://{shared_bucket}/{train_qa_key}"
metadata_s3 = f"s3://{shared_bucket}/{metadata_key}"
chunks_s3_uri = f"s3://{bucket_name}/{chunks_s3_key}"

def smart_read_csv(path: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Read a CSV as utf-8, falling back to latin-1 for the odd accented author name."""
    try:
        return pd.read_csv(path)
    except UnicodeDecodeError:
        return pd.read_csv(path, encoding="latin-1")

    Then download the three files, skipping any already on disk, and load them so we can check the counts before spending GPU time on them.

    PYTHON 

    train_qa_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "train_QA.csv")
metadata_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "metadata.csv")
local_chunks_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "chunks.jsonl")

if not os.path.exists(train_qa_path):
    s3_client.download_file(shared_bucket, train_qa_key, train_qa_path)
if not os.path.exists(metadata_path):
    s3_client.download_file(shared_bucket, metadata_key, metadata_path)
if not os.path.exists(local_chunks_path):
    s3_client.download_file(bucket_name, chunks_s3_key, local_chunks_path)   # written by the Bedrock episode

train_df = smart_read_csv(train_qa_path)
metadata_df = smart_read_csv(metadata_path)
with open(local_chunks_path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    chunked_docs = [json.loads(line) for line in f]

print("Train QAs:", len(train_df))
print("Metadata rows:", len(metadata_df))
print("Chunks:", len(chunked_docs), "from", chunks_s3_uri)
train_df.head(3)

    If the last download fails with NoSuchKey, go back to the Bedrock episode and run its chunking step; this episode starts from its output.

    Step 2 – Processing Job 1: embed all chunks on a GPU

    Now we launch a short-lived Hugging Face Processing job that:

    1. Downloads chunks.jsonl from S3.
    2. Loads thenlper/gte-large from Hugging Face with the container’s own transformers.
    3. Encodes each chunk into an embedding vector.
    4. Saves the full matrix as embeddings.npy back to S3.

    We use the same embedding_inference.py script across projects; here it expects a JSONL file with a text field.

    Nothing to install

    Neither job installs anything. The Hugging Face container ships transformers and PyTorch, which is all the embedding wrapper and the generator need, so both jobs start as soon as the instance is up. A requirements.txt next to a script would be pip-installed before it runs; neither job here has one.

    Cost tracking: tag every job

    Tags do not propagate in AWS. The tags you put on your notebook instance cover the notebook’s hourly cost and nothing else. Each Processing job below launches its own GPU instance, which is a separate billable resource with no tags unless we pass them at launch, as with the training and tuning jobs earlier in the workshop. An untagged job shows up in Cost Explorer as anonymous SageMaker spend that nobody can attribute to a team.

    Define the tags once and pass tags=job_tags to every HuggingFaceProcessor you create. Use a distinct Purpose per job so you can tell the embedding job from the batch RAG job on the bill.

    PYTHON 

    name = "DoeJohn"         # replace with your name
project = "SinkOrSwim"   # your challenge: WattBot2026, BadgerScribe, BadgerCode, BrainDecoding, PoisonedWell or SnapshotWI; SinkOrSwim is the workshop itself

import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "/home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts")
import helpers   # check_launch: the account's rules, with a message that names the problem

def make_job_tags(purpose: str):   # one of: Storage, Notebook, Training, Tuning, Inference
    return helpers.check_launch([   # checked against the account's rules first, with a message that names the problem
        {"Key": "Name", "Value": name},
        {"Key": "Project", "Value": project},
        {"Key": "Purpose", "Value": purpose},   # differs per job so the bill tells them apart
    ])

print("Tags on every job this episode launches:", make_job_tags("Inference"))   # check them before launching: a job tagged DoeJohn is on the bill as DoeJohn

    Launch the embedding job

    Open scripts/embedding_inference.py first; it is under fifty lines. It reads a JSONL file of chunks from the job’s input directory, embeds them with whatever Hugging Face model --model_id names, through the thirty-line wrapper in hf_embedder.py, normalises the vectors so a dot product is a cosine similarity, and saves one embeddings.npy to the output directory. Nothing in it knows about WattBot. Inputs in, outputs out, no state.

    A HuggingFaceProcessor is the Processing-job counterpart of the estimator, with the same role, tags, instance type and container versions, plus a runtime cap. Its run call names the script, mounts the inputs, and says where the output goes. Once it is launched, the job appears on the Processing jobs page of the SageMaker console (under Data preparation in the left menu), the Processing counterpart of the Training jobs page you used earlier.

    In class the instructor has run this job already and staged its output. The switch below copies that matrix into your bucket, at the key the job would have written, and the launch cell then skips the job. The second job, which you do launch, has the same shape and is where the class spends its GPU minutes. On your own, set it to False and run the job; it is eight minutes.

    PYTHON 

    def _s3_object_exists(bucket: str, key: str) -> bool:
    try:
        s3_client.head_object(Bucket=bucket, Key=key)
        return True
    except s3_client.exceptions.ClientError:
        return False

embedding_model_id = "thenlper/gte-large"
emb_output_prefix = "wattbot/embeddings"
emb_output_path = f"s3://{bucket_name}/{emb_output_prefix}/"

use_instructor_embeddings = True                       # True in class: copy the instructor's gte-large matrix and skip the job. False: run the job
shared_gte_key = "wattbot/embeddings_gte_large.npy"    # where the instructor staged it in the shared bucket

run_embedding_job = not (use_instructor_embeddings and _s3_object_exists(shared_bucket, shared_gte_key))
if not run_embedding_job:
    s3_client.copy({"Bucket": shared_bucket, "Key": shared_gte_key}, bucket_name, f"{emb_output_prefix}/embeddings.npy")
    print(f"Copied the instructor's embeddings to s3://{bucket_name}/{emb_output_prefix}/embeddings.npy; the embedding job is skipped")

    PYTHON 

    
embedding_processor = HuggingFaceProcessor(
    base_job_name="WattBot-embed-gte-large",   # SageMaker appends a timestamp to make each job name unique
    role=role,
    tags=make_job_tags("Inference"),   # tags are per job; nothing is inherited from the notebook
    instance_type="ml.g5.xlarge",      # the GPU the job rents (A10G, 24 GB): plenty for a 335M-parameter embedder
    instance_count=1,
    transformers_version="4.56",       # these three pick the prebuilt container image
    pytorch_version="2.8",
    py_version="py312",
    sagemaker_session=session,
    max_runtime_in_seconds=2 * 60 * 60,   # 2 hours, in seconds (2 h x 60 min x 60 s); the estimate is ~8 minutes. SageMaker kills the job here, so a hang costs at most this
)

if run_embedding_job:   # False in class when the instructor's matrix was copied in above
    # run() uploads the code, starts the instance, streams the job's log here and returns when the script ends (wait=True is the default)
    start = time.time()
    embedding_processor.run(
        code="embedding_inference.py",     # the script the container runs...
        source_dir="code_embed/",          # ...uploaded with everything beside it (hf_embedder.py)
        inputs=[
            ProcessingInput(
                source=chunks_s3_uri,                       # S3 object (or prefix) copied in before the script starts
                destination="/opt/ml/processing/input",    # where it appears inside the container
            )
        ],
        outputs=[
            ProcessingOutput(
                output_name="embeddings",
                source="/opt/ml/processing/output",        # whatever the script writes here...
                destination=emb_output_path,               # ...is copied to this S3 prefix when the script ends
            )
        ],
        arguments=[                        # command-line flags, as the script's argparse expects them
            "--model_id", embedding_model_id,
            "--input_filename", "chunks.jsonl",
            "--text_key", "text",
            "--input_dir", "/opt/ml/processing/input",
            "--output_dir", "/opt/ml/processing/output",
        ],
    )

    print(f"Embedding job complete: {(time.time() - start) / 60:.1f} min wall-clock, including instance startup")

    Check on the running job in the AWS Console

    In the console the job is under SageMaker AI → Data preparation → Processing jobs, or at this link for the class region (change us-east-2 in it for another region).

    It takes about 10 minutes in total for the job to complete, a couple of provisioning the instance and downloading the embedding model, eight of embedding. That startup is the cost of a job, paid once. The embedding job runs once per corpus, and the GPU bills only while it runs.

    Sanity-check the embeddings locally

    We can download embeddings.npy back into the notebook and inspect its shape to confirm the job ran successfully.

    PYTHON 

    local_embeddings_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "embeddings.npy")
embeddings_key = f"{emb_output_prefix}/embeddings.npy"   # the ProcessingOutput destination + the filename the script wrote

s3_client.download_file(bucket_name, embeddings_key, local_embeddings_path)
chunk_embeddings = np.load(local_embeddings_path)

print("Embeddings shape:", chunk_embeddings.shape, "for", len(chunked_docs), "chunks")

    Step 3 – Processing Job 2: the WattBot RAG loop as a job

    For the second job, we pass four inputs:

    • chunks.jsonl – serialized chunks (your bucket)
    • embeddings.npy – precomputed chunk embeddings (your bucket, written by Job 1)
    • train_QA.csv – training questions (shared bucket)
    • metadata.csv – to resolve ref_id → URL (shared bucket)

    The --per_type 10 argument draws the same stratified sample the Bedrock episode scored, ten questions per evidence type with the same seed, so the two runs are compared on the same questions; leave it out to answer them all. Open scripts/wattbot_rag_batch.py and read main before launching it. It is short, because the pipeline lives in scripts/wattbot_rag.py, the same module the Bedrock episode imported:

    • retrieve_top_k: cosine similarity over the embedding matrix
    • run_single_qa: retrieval, the answer call, the hybrid unanswerable rule (retrieval threshold OR the model’s own is_blank), the explanation call
    • compute_wattbot_score: the metric we use at the end

    What the batch script adds is the two model callables. embed_query wraps the same gte-large model and pooling the embedding job used (hf_embedder.py) (the question has to be embedded with the same model as the chunks), and generate_batch wraps transformers.generate on the generator (Qwen3-8B here) with Qwen’s thinking mode off, taking several prompts at once. The loop itself is run_batch_qa, the batched twin of the run_single_qa the Bedrock episode used, with the same retrieval, prompts and unanswerable rule, with the model calls grouped four at a time because a GPU decoding one prompt is idle most of the time. The group is a trade. More prompts at once is faster, and each one adds its own cache of attention keys and values to the 16 GB the weights already hold, so a group of long prompts can run the 24 GB card out of memory. The script halves the group and retries when that happens, so a long batch costs time, not the job. The job writes wattbot_solutions.csv in the WattBot submission format.

    Callout

    Why not vLLM?

    vLLM is the open-source inference engine most people serve open-weight models with. You give it a model name, it loads the weights onto the GPU and answers chat requests, batching many at once so that throughput scales. That is what you want behind an API with users. This job has about 100 prompts and no users waiting, and transformers.generate, already in the container, can decode several prompts at once too. run_batch_qa in wattbot_rag.py hands them to the model four at a time (--batch_size), which is where most of vLLM’s speed on a batch like this comes from, with nothing to install. vLLM’s install is several gigabytes of billed GPU time before the first answer. The GPU-notebook episode uses vLLM, where its 8-bit weights are needed to fit a larger model.

    PYTHON 

    emb_output_s3 = f"s3://{bucket_name}/{emb_output_prefix}/embeddings.npy"

print("chunks:    ", chunks_s3_uri)
print("embeddings:", emb_output_s3)
print("train_QA:  ", train_qa_s3)
print("metadata:  ", metadata_s3)

    If the launch is refused with an AccessDeniedException ending in explicit deny, the account’s checks are the cause: a missing tag, an instance type outside the lesson’s list, or a resource kind the lesson never creates; the first training episode’s callout If the launch is refused says what to look at. If the launch below fails at once with ResourceLimitExceeded naming an instance type, nothing in the notebook is wrong. The account’s quota for that type is too low, and the increase is requested in Service Quotas (days, for GPU types). On your own account, request ml.g5.xlarge for processing job usage before you start.

    What launching a job means

    This is the first GPU job you launch yourself in this episode (the embedding job above was staged for you in class), so this is what happens when you launch one. You describe a machine and point at a script. SageMaker rents the machine, copies the files you named from S3 onto its disk, runs your script on it, copies whatever the script wrote in its output folder back to S3, and shuts the machine down. The notebook does nothing but wait and show you the script’s printed output. Nothing from this notebook’s memory goes along, not chunked_docs, not train_df, not any function defined above. The script sees only the files you copied in and the arguments you gave it, which is why every input is an S3 location and every setting is a command-line flag. That is the same thing estimator.fit did in the fine-tuning episode, with one difference. A training job hands back a trained model, a Processing job hands back whatever files the script wrote, here a CSV of answers.

    The description is two cells. The first builds a HuggingFaceProcessor, saying which machine, which container image, how long it may run, whose tags it carries. Two of its settings matter more than on the embedding job. volume_size_in_gb=60 attaches a 60 GB volume to the instance, mounted under /opt/ml/processing; the container’s own root disk is small, so the 16 GB of model weights must not land there. env= sets two environment variables in the container. HF_HOME points Hugging Face’s download cache at that volume, which is where the weights go, and PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF tells PyTorch to reuse freed GPU memory in place instead of leaving it fragmented, which matters when a batch of prompts is close to what the card holds.

    PYTHON 

    rag_output_prefix = "wattbot/solutions"                       # where this job's output lands in your bucket
rag_output_path = f"s3://{bucket_name}/{rag_output_prefix}/"

generation_model_id = "Qwen/Qwen3-8B"   # the Hugging Face name the job downloads; ~16 GB of bf16 weights

rag_processor = HuggingFaceProcessor(
    base_job_name="WattBot-rag-batch",   # SageMaker appends a timestamp; this is the name you look for on the Processing jobs page
    role=role,                           # the IAM role the job runs under, to read your bucket and the shared one
    tags=make_job_tags("Inference"),     # separate job, separate tags: nothing is inherited from the embedding job
    instance_type="ml.g5.xlarge",        # 1 x A10G, 24 GB: holds the bf16 8B model plus the KV cache
    instance_count=1,
    volume_size_in_gb=60,                # disk attached to the instance, mounted at /opt/ml/processing; the weights go here
    env={"HF_HOME": "/opt/ml/processing/hf_cache",                  # environment variables in the container: Hugging Face downloads to this path...
         "PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF": "expandable_segments:True"},   # ...and PyTorch reuses freed GPU memory instead of fragmenting it, which is what a batch of long prompts runs out of
    transformers_version="4.56",         # these three pick the prebuilt container image, the same one the embedding job used
    pytorch_version="2.8",
    py_version="py312",
    sagemaker_session=session,
    max_runtime_in_seconds=2 * 60 * 60,  # the cap: SageMaker kills the job after 2 hours; the estimate is 20 minutes
)

    The processor is only a description; nothing runs until run. Its arguments are the three things a job needs, the code (code and source_dir), the data (inputs, each an S3 location and the container path it is copied to before the script starts), and where the results go (outputs, a container path copied to S3 when the script ends). The arguments list is the script’s command line, in the form its argparse expects.

    PYTHON 

    start = time.time()
rag_processor.run(
    code="wattbot_rag_batch.py",       # the script the container runs...
    source_dir="code_rag/",            # ...uploaded with everything beside it: wattbot_rag.py and hf_embedder.py, which it imports
    inputs=[                           # each input: an S3 object, and the container path it is copied to before the script starts
        ProcessingInput(
            source=chunks_s3_uri,                              # the chunks, from your bucket
            destination="/opt/ml/processing/input/chunks",     # four inputs, each in its own subdirectory
        ),
        ProcessingInput(
            source=emb_output_s3,                              # the gte-large matrix the embedding job wrote
            destination="/opt/ml/processing/input/embeddings",
        ),
        ProcessingInput(
            source=train_qa_s3,                                # the questions, from the shared bucket
            destination="/opt/ml/processing/input/train",
        ),
        ProcessingInput(
            source=metadata_s3,                                # the paper index, to fill the ref_url column
            destination="/opt/ml/processing/input/metadata",
        ),
    ],
    outputs=[
        ProcessingOutput(
            output_name="solutions",
            source="/opt/ml/processing/output",                # whatever the script writes here...
            destination=rag_output_path,                       # ...is copied to this S3 prefix when the script ends
        )
    ],
    arguments=[                        # the script's command line: python wattbot_rag_batch.py --input_dir ... --top_k 8 ...
        "--input_dir", "/opt/ml/processing/input",             # where the inputs above were mounted
        "--output_dir", "/opt/ml/processing/output",           # where the script must write for the output copy to pick it up
        "--embedding_model_id", embedding_model_id,            # the same model that embedded the chunks, to embed each question
        "--qwen_model_id", generation_model_id,                # the generator
        "--top_k", "8",                                        # chunks handed to the model per question
        "--retrieval_threshold", "0.25",                       # best cosine below this => unanswerable
        "--per_type", "10",                                    # the same stratified sample the Bedrock episode scored (seed 0); drop it for all the questions
        "--batch_size", "4",                                   # prompts decoded together; 1 would be one at a time, several times slower. 8 ran out of GPU memory on long prompts
    ],
)

print(f"RAG batch job complete: {(time.time() - start) / 60:.1f} min wall-clock, including instance startup and the weight download")

    While it runs, read what the container is printing. Open the Processing jobs page, click the job’s name, scroll to Monitor and click View logs. That opens CloudWatch, the AWS service that stores every job’s printed output, at a list with one entry named after your job; click it. The text is the container’s stdout, kept after the job ends, updated while it runs (refresh). You will see, in order, Loading model with transformers, the weight download (16 GB in shards), a line per batch of answers and of explanations, then one line per question. The whole job is the 15 minutes in the cost callout; the generation is the last six of them.

    Step 4 – Download predictions and evaluate

    Finally, we download wattbot_solutions.csv from S3, inspect a few rows, and compute the WattBot score against train_QA.csv with the same compute_wattbot_score the Bedrock episode used.

    PYTHON 

    solutions_key = f"{rag_output_prefix}/wattbot_solutions.csv"
local_solutions_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "wattbot_solutions.csv")

s3_client.download_file(bucket_name, solutions_key, local_solutions_path)
solutions_df = pd.read_csv(local_solutions_path)
solutions_df.head()

    Score the predictions with the competition’s own Score.py, through the same wrapper the Bedrock episode used, so the two runs compare directly.

    PYTHON 

    from wattbot_rag import compute_wattbot_score

results_df = compute_wattbot_score(
    train_qa_path=train_qa_path,
    preds_path=local_solutions_path,
    n_examples=10,
)

    Compare the overall score with the Bedrock run. The retrieval logic, prompts and scoring are identical, so any difference is the two models, gte-large versus Titan for retrieval, Qwen3-8B versus DeepSeek V3 for generation. In one run on the same 53 questions, Qwen3-8B scored 0.54 against DeepSeek V3’s 0.69. Its citations were better (F1 0.70 against 0.60) and its answers worse (47% against 70% correct), with the cross-paper and calculation questions losing the most, a fifth of each right against three fifths. An 8B model against a 671B one is not a fair fight, and the gap is the price of a model you host yourself on one small GPU.

    Challenge

    What did the two jobs cost?

    Ask SageMaker what it recorded for each job. session.sagemaker_client.describe_processing_job(ProcessingJobName=...) returns CreationTime, ProcessingStartTime and ProcessingEndTime. The job names are embedding_processor.latest_job.job_name and rag_processor.latest_job.job_name. For each job, compute the minutes between creation and start (provisioning, before the instance is billed) and between start and end (the billed window), and price the billed window at $1.41/h, the ml.g5.xlarge rate both jobs used. Then, from the RAG job’s CloudWatch log timestamps, estimate how much of its billed window was setup (the weight download and model load) and how much was generation. How does the total compare with the cost callout, and with the Bedrock run?

    describe_processing_job returns three timestamps; the gap between the first two is unbilled provisioning, between the last two the billed run.

    PYTHON 

    def job_cost(job_name: str, price_per_hour: float):
    d = session.sagemaker_client.describe_processing_job(ProcessingJobName=job_name)   # the record SageMaker keeps for the job
    # CreationTime -> ProcessingStartTime: provisioning the instance, not billed
    provisioning = (d["ProcessingStartTime"] - d["CreationTime"]).total_seconds() / 60
    # ProcessingStartTime -> ProcessingEndTime: the script running, billed by the second
    billed = (d["ProcessingEndTime"] - d["ProcessingStartTime"]).total_seconds() / 60
    cost = billed / 60 * price_per_hour
    print(f"{job_name}: {d['ProcessingJobStatus']}")
    print(f"  wall-clock:                {provisioning + billed:.1f} min from launch to end")
    print(f"  provisioning (not billed): {provisioning:.1f} min")
    print(f"  billed window:             {billed:.1f} min at ${price_per_hour}/h = ${cost:.2f}")
    print(f"  output:                    {d['ProcessingOutputConfig']['Outputs'][0]['S3Output']['S3Uri']}")   # where the job's files went
    return cost

total = job_cost(embedding_processor.latest_job.job_name, 1.41) if run_embedding_job else 0.0   # no job to price when the matrix was copied in
total += job_cost(rag_processor.latest_job.job_name, 1.41)
print(f"GPU total for the episode: ${total:.2f}")

    Expect the embedding job to bill about 8 minutes (about $0.20) and the RAG job about 14 minutes (about $0.32), so about $0.50 of GPU time, the callout’s GPU figure. In the RAG job’s log, the first 8 minutes of the billed window are the download and the model load; the last 6 are the questions, two generation calls each. Setup is more than half of what you paid for, which is the argument for keeping an HF_HOME cache on S3 (skip the download) once a job is run routinely. The Bedrock run of the same questions cost cents, and the self-hosted route is only justified here because the model is not in the catalog.

    Challenge

    What a shorter runtime cap would have done

    Both processors set max_runtime_in_seconds=2 * 60 * 60. Predict what would happen if the RAG job were launched with max_runtime_in_seconds=600 instead. What does the job status become, what is in the output prefix, and what did it cost? Then compute the most a hung job can bill under the cap each job set, and compare it with the cost of an ml.g6e.xlarge notebook instance left running over a weekend (64 hours).

    With a 600-second cap the RAG job is killed by SageMaker ten minutes after ProcessingStartTime, while it is still downloading or loading the weights. The status becomes Stopped (the failure reason reads MaxRuntimeExceeded), the output prefix is empty because the script never reached the point of writing wattbot_solutions.csv, and the bill is the full 600 seconds, 600 / 3600 × $1.41 ≈ $0.24 for nothing. A cap has to leave room for the setup that precedes the work, which is why ours is six times the 20-minute estimate, not ten percent over it.

    Under the caps we set, the worst case for a job that hangs (a stuck download, a model that never finishes loading) is 2 h × $1.41 = $2.82 for either job. An ml.g6e.xlarge notebook instance forgotten over a weekend is 64 h × $2.61 = $167, and nothing caps it.

    Key Points
    • Bedrock’s catalog is curated and lags releases; when you need a specific open-weight model you rent a GPU and serve it yourself.
    • Of the ways to rent a GPU, a Processing job is the one that cannot be forgotten. It bills while the script runs and ends on its own, with max_runtime_in_seconds as the backstop. Use it for batch work; use Bedrock or an endpoint when you need answers in seconds.
    • Inference needs only the weights. Qwen3-8B in bf16 is ~16 GB and fits one 24 GB GPU, with the rest for the prompts’ attention cache; how many prompts decode together is bounded by that remainder.
    • A job’s inputs and outputs are S3 prefixes mounted into the container; the notebook only stages files and reads results, so it stays a cheap CPU instance.
    • The pipeline logic (wattbot_rag.py) ships with the job unchanged from the Bedrock episode; only the two model callables differ.
    • Tags do not propagate from the notebook. Every job gets its own tags=.

    Content from (Optional) RAG with a Notebook GPU

    Last updated on 2026-10-28 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 45 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How can we run a basic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline entirely from a single GPU-backed SageMaker notebook?
    • How do we go from cached text chunks to a searchable embedding space using a self-hosted model?
    • How can we generate WattBot-style answers (including citations and evidence) that follow the competition’s scoring conventions?

    Objectives

    • Verify that our SageMaker notebook instance has a working GPU and compatible Python environment.
    • Reuse the WattBot metadata and questions from the shared bucket, and the chunks.jsonl the Bedrock episode cached in your own bucket.
    • Build the embedding matrix and the retrieval step with a self-hosted embedding model, in plain NumPy.
    • Build a small retrieval helper that finds the most relevant chunks for a question using cosine similarity in embedding space.
    • Serve a 27B open-weight generator (Qwen3.8-27B in FP8, via vLLM) on the notebook’s GPU and wire it to the retriever to produce WattBot-format answers (including answer, ref_id, ref_url, and supporting_materials).
    • Explain why inference uses quantized weights instead of bf16, and what a self-hosted GPU costs per hour, per forgotten weekend, and per forgotten month.
    • Add a second LLM pass that generates short explanations and marks whether the evidence comes from text, figures, tables, or a combination.
    Callout

    Optional, self-study episode

    This episode is not taught in the workshop. The Bedrock and Processing Jobs episodes are the default ways to run RAG; this one is for the case where you need to work on a self-hosted model by hand, and only if you will remember to stop the instance. Do not run this notebook on the controller instance from the other episodes. Create a new GPU notebook instance for it (Setup below). On a CPU instance the vLLM install and the 27 GB model load will exhaust memory and freeze your JupyterLab. It runs the same pipeline as the Processing Jobs episode on a GPU notebook instance, which is the right tool for prototyping alone at a keyboard and the wrong one for a room of a hundred people with meters running. Work through it on your own when you want to see model loading, GPU memory and generation as plain Python. Read the cost callout first.

    Why run RAG on a GPU notebook?

    The Bedrock and Processing Jobs episodes are the better patterns for most research work. Bedrock serves the models for you, and a Processing job rents a GPU only long enough to finish a batch. A notebook GPU gives you something different, an interactive place to load a model, watch GPU memory, try retrieval strategies and change prompts without repackaging a job after every experiment.

    That matters when you need a model Bedrock does not offer and want to work on it by hand. This episode runs the WattBot pipeline with Qwen3.8-27B as the generator, a 27-billion-parameter open-weight (Apache 2.0) model released in August 2026 that Bedrock does not carry, loaded in FP8 through vLLM beside a local embedding model. Everything a managed model API hides, loading an embedding model, loading a generator, fitting both in GPU memory, is a cell you can run and change.

    A 27B model is large enough that the choice of GPU and weight precision matters. At about one byte per weight, FP8 puts the weights near 27 GB, and a 48 GB L40S leaves room for the embedding model and the attention cache that generation needs. The 24 GB GPU the earlier episodes used cannot hold this setup. That makes the notebook a good place to learn about model serving, and an expensive place to leave idle.

    Treat this as an interactive experiment, not a deployment pattern. Create the separate GPU notebook described below. Do not run it on the CPU controller from the other episodes.

    Callout

    This instance bills $2.61 an hour until you stop it, and nothing stops it for you

    A GPU notebook instance is a rental with the meter running. It bills by the hour from the moment it starts until the moment you stop it, whether it is generating answers, sitting at an idle prompt, or showing a closed browser tab on a laptop that went home for the weekend. Nothing in this episode turns it off for you. The instance we use, ml.g6e.xlarge (one L40S GPU, 48 GB), costs $2.61 per hour on-demand in us-east-1 (AWS price list, October 2026). That is:

    Left running for Cost
    This episode (~2 hours) ~$5
    Overnight (12 h) ~$31
    A weekend (64 h) ~$167
    A week ~$438
    A month ~$1,906

    The same evaluation on Bedrock cost well under a dollar. One forgotten weekend on this instance costs a thousand times more than the work it was rented for. A forgotten GPU notebook is the most common way research groups overspend cloud credits.

    Two further charges people do not expect:

    • A stopped instance still bills for its storage. We give this notebook a 100 GB volume for model weights. SageMaker charges $0.14 per GB-month for notebook storage, so a stopped-but-not-deleted instance costs about $14 a month forever. When you are done with the episode, delete the instance, not just stop it, unless you will use it again within days.
    • Idle is billed the same as busy. There is no discount for a GPU that is loaded and waiting. Loading a 27B model takes a few minutes, which tempts people to leave the instance up “so I don’t have to reload”. That is the $1,906.

    What keeps this safe:

    1. Stop the instance when you stand up, every time, from the Notebook instances page (select it, Stop). Then look at the status column until it says Stopped.
    2. Set a reminder on your phone or calendar before you start the instance, for two hours from now.
    3. Prefer jobs for anything beyond exploration: a Processing job (the Processing Jobs episode) or a training job ends on its own, and max_runtime_in_seconds (max_run on a training job) guarantees it.

    What we’ll build

    We reuse the WattBot 2026 document chunks and evaluation questions prepared in the Bedrock episode. The pipeline keeps its purpose. What changes is that its two managed model calls become two models running on this GPU, thenlper/gte-large for embeddings and Qwen3.8-27B for answers. Qwen3.8-27B is the newer and larger relative of the Qwen3-8B the Processing Jobs episode ran, and sits within a few points of a frontier commercial model on agent tasks and science questions (see that episode’s chart), which is why it is worth the trouble of hosting.

    First we load the cached chunks and embed them into a searchable matrix. Then we implement cosine-similarity retrieval so a question brings back the most relevant passages. Finally we load Qwen through vLLM, pass those passages into the same WattBot prompts, and generate answers, citations and short explanations that label the evidence type, [text], [table], [figure] or a combination such as [text+table]. Scoring those answers against the competition’s references tells us how the self-hosted pipeline performs, not only whether it runs.

    The workflow is kept close to the earlier episodes on purpose. With the documents, prompts and scoring the same, the differences in model serving are the only thing left to compare.

    Notebook + dataset setup

    For this episode you need a notebook instance with a GPU that can hold the FP8 27B model plus the embedding model plus working memory for generation. Create a new notebook instance (same steps as the controller-notebook episode, same three tags) with:

    • Instance type: ml.g6e.xlarge (1 × L40S, 48 GB GPU memory, $2.61/h on the Instances for ML page). The FP8 weights are ~27 GB; the rest is for the embedding model and the KV cache that generation needs for long prompts. The L40S runs FP8 natively. A 24 GB instance such as ml.g5.xlarge cannot hold this model; a 16 GB ml.g4dn.xlarge cannot hold anything in this size class.
    • Volume size: 100 GB (the default of 5 GB will not fit the weights or the vLLM install). This volume bills at $0.14 per GB-month even while the instance is stopped.
    • Tags: the same Project, Name, Purpose keys as every other resource; Purpose is Notebook.

    Once it is InService, open JupyterLab, clone the lesson repository as in the controller-notebook episode (this is a new instance, so it has no copy yet), and open /ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/notebooks/13_RAG-GPU-notebook.ipynb. Select the conda_pytorch kernel.

    See Instances for ML for further guidance. This instance bills by the hour from the moment it starts, whether or not it is doing anything. Stop it when you leave, and delete it when the episode is over.

    Install vLLM first

    The install may replace PyTorch and then needs a kernel restart, so it comes before anything is loaded.

    Callout

    Installing vLLM takes a few minutes, and the meter is running

    vLLM is the open-source inference engine that loads an open-weight model onto the GPU and answers chat requests from Python, the self-hosted counterpart of Bedrock’s runtime (the Processing Jobs episode introduces it). pip install vllm downloads several gigabytes (it brings its own CUDA kernels and may replace the kernel’s PyTorch build) and takes 5–10 minutes. Qwen3.8 needs vLLM 0.17 or newer. The 27 GB of model weights take another 4–6 minutes to download the first time. At $2.61 an hour that is about 60 cents of waiting, which is fine; what is not fine is doing it twice because the instance was deleted and recreated. Keep the Hugging Face cache on the 100 GB volume (the HF_HOME line in the serving cell below does that) so the weights survive a stop/start.

    def download_s3_object(bucket: str, key: str, local_path: str) -> None:

    Step 1 – Model libraries and safe CSV loading

    PYTHON 

    import torch
from hf_embedder import HFEmbedder   # thirty lines on plain transformers: encode(list of strings) -> unit-length matrix; the Processing jobs use the same file

    A CSV reader that tries a few encodings, because some metadata files are not valid UTF-8.

    PYTHON 

    def smart_read_csv(path: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Try several encodings when reading a CSV file.

    Some CSVs (especially those with special characters in author names or titles)
    may not be valid UTF-8. This helper rotates through common encodings and raises
    the last error only if all fail.
    """
    encodings = ["utf-8", "latin1", "ISO-8859-1", "cp1252"]
    last_error = None
    for enc in encodings:
        try:
            return pd.read_csv(path, encoding=enc)
        except Exception as e:
            last_error = e
    if last_error is not None:
        raise last_error
    raise RuntimeError(f"Unable to read CSV at {path}")


train_df = smart_read_csv(train_qa_path)
metadata_df = smart_read_csv(metadata_path)

print("train_QA.csv columns:", train_df.columns.tolist())
print("metadata.csv columns:", metadata_df.columns.tolist())
print("\nNumber of training QAs:", len(train_df))
print("Number of metadata rows:", len(metadata_df))

train_df.head(15)

chunks_jsonl_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "chunks.jsonl")

def load_chunked_docs_jsonl(path):

if not os.path.exists(chunks_jsonl_path):
