    Each chunk keeps a pointer back to its document and page metadata (doc_id, title, url, page_num, page_label, chunk_idx_in_page), which we use later to cite sources.

    Step 3 – Build an embedding matrix

    Now we embed each chunk into a vector with an open embedding model:

    thenlper/gte-large

    The embedder the Processing Jobs episode used has 335 million parameters, 0.7 GB in bf16, 1,024-dimensional vectors, and about 1,100 chunks a minute on an A10G, so the 9,000 chunks here take a few minutes on this GPU.

    We will:

    1. Load the embedding model on GPU if available.
    2. Encode all chunks in batches.
    3. Store the resulting matrix as a torch.Tensor or numpy.ndarray along with the original chunked_docs list.

    Later, we’ll implement a small retrieval helper that does cosine-similarity search over this matrix, with no indexing library.

    PYTHON 

    # We'll use a stronger embedding model now that we have a GPU.
# This model has ~335M parameters and benefits from GPU acceleration,
# and fits beside the 27B generator on this 48 GB GPU.
embedding_model_id = "thenlper/gte-large"

print("CUDA available for embeddings:", torch.cuda.is_available())

# Single shared embedder object that we can pass around; it uses the GPU when one is available
embedder = HFEmbedder(embedding_model_id)

    Embed every chunk in batches on the GPU and stack the results into one matrix, one row per chunk.

    PYTHON 

    def embed_texts(embedder, docs, batch_size: int = 32) -> np.ndarray:
    """Embed all chunk texts into a dense matrix of shape (N, D)."""
    texts = [d["text"] for d in docs]
    all_embeddings = []
    start = time.time()
    for i in range(0, len(texts), batch_size):
        batch = texts[i : i + batch_size]
        emb = embedder.encode(
            batch,
            convert_to_numpy=True,
            show_progress_bar=False,
            normalize_embeddings=True,   # unit-length vectors, so a dot product is the cosine similarity
        )
        all_embeddings.append(emb)
    embeddings = np.vstack(all_embeddings) if all_embeddings else np.zeros((0, 1024))
    print(f"Computed embeddings for {len(texts)} chunks in {time.time() - start:.1f}s")
    return embeddings

    PYTHON 

    
chunk_embeddings = embed_texts(embedder, chunked_docs)
chunk_embeddings.shape

    4. Build a simple retrieval step (cosine similarity)

    Retrieval here is cosine similarity between the question’s vector and every chunk’s vector, with the top k chunks as context, and nothing more. For nine thousand chunks that is one matrix multiply. A vector database (FAISS, Chroma, Weaviate) is the same step built for millions of chunks or many concurrent users, with approximate search, metadata filters and a shared index; swapping it in changes nothing else in the pipeline.

    retrieve_top_k from wattbot_rag.py is that search. Normalize the query and the matrix, one matrix multiply for the cosine similarities, argsort for the top k. Open the file to see it; it is a dozen lines. embed_query_with wraps the embedder as the embed_query(question) callable the rest of the pipeline expects.

    PYTHON 

    embed_query = embed_query_with(embedder)   # embed_query(question) -> vector, with the same model that embedded the chunks

# Quick sanity check for `retrieve_top_k` on the first training question
first_row = train_df.iloc[0]
test_question = first_row["question"]
print("Sample question:", test_question)

test_retrieved = retrieve_top_k(
    query_embedding=embed_query(test_question),
    chunk_embeddings=chunk_embeddings,
    chunked_docs=chunked_docs,
    k=3,
)

print(f"Top {len(test_retrieved)} retrieved chunks:")
for r in test_retrieved:
    snippet = r["text"].replace("\n", " ")
    if len(snippet) > 160:
        snippet = snippet[:160] + "..."
    print(f"- score={r['score']:.3f} | doc_id={r['doc_id']} | page={r['page_label']} | snippet={snippet}")

    5. Serve the generator, Qwen3.8-27B in FP8, with vLLM

    For this episode we use Qwen3.8-27B, an open-weight model that Bedrock does not carry, in its FP8 release (Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8), served with vLLM. It is a dense 27B model with a hybrid attention design (most layers use a linear-attention variant with a fixed-size state, so the KV cache stays small even for long prompts), a native 262K context, and a “thinking” mode that is on by default and that we turn off, because WattBot wants a JSON answer, not a reasoning trace.

    Why FP8 weights and not bf16? Inference is not training. No gradients, no optimizer state, nothing is updated, so the only memory that matters is the weights themselves plus the KV cache for the prompt being processed. A 27B model in bf16 is about 54 GB of weights and does not fit a 48 GB GPU; the same weights in 8-bit floating point are about 27 GB, which fits with room for the embedding model and generation. FP8 is near-lossless for a model this size, and it is faster, because decoding is limited by how fast the GPU can read weights from memory. For inference on rented GPUs, reduced-precision weights are the norm (FP8 where the GPU supports it, 4-bit integer where it does not or where memory is tighter); bf16 is what you use when you have memory to spare and a model small enough not to need it.

    Why vLLM and not transformers.pipeline? vLLM is an inference server. It has the kernels for FP8 and for this model’s hybrid attention, batches requests, and manages the KV cache so long prompts do not run out of memory. It is what you would deploy behind an API, and its offline LLM class is a two-line replacement for a transformers.pipeline.

    We will:

    1. Call the model once to propose an answer and supporting evidence.
    2. Call it a second time with a smaller prompt to generate a short explanation (<= 100 characters).

    PYTHON 

    import os
# Keep model weights on the notebook's 100 GB volume, not the small root disk.

from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

qwen_model_id = "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8"   # pre-quantized FP8 checkpoint; vLLM reads that from its config, so no quantization= argument is needed

load_start = time.time()
llm = LLM(
    model=qwen_model_id,                         # Hugging Face id; the weights download to HF_HOME on first use
    max_model_len=8192,                          # longest prompt + answer we need; the model allows 262K, we do not
    gpu_memory_utilization=0.85,                 # leave ~7 GB for the embedding model and PyTorch overhead
    limit_mm_per_prompt={"image": 0, "video": 0},  # text only: skip reserving memory for the vision encoder
)
print(f"Model loaded in {(time.time() - load_start) / 60:.1f} min (download on first use, then weights into GPU memory)")
print("vLLM engine ready:", qwen_model_id)

    PYTHON 

    !nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.total --format=csv

    The number above is what you are paying for, a 48 GB GPU, most of it now holding model weights and a reserved KV cache. It stays allocated, and billed, until you stop the instance.

    PYTHON 

    def call_qwen_chat(system_prompt: str, user_prompt: str, max_new_tokens: int = 384) -> str:
    """Send a chat prompt to the vLLM engine and return only the generated text."""
    messages = [
        {"role": "system", "content": system_prompt},
        {"role": "user", "content": user_prompt},
    ]
    params = SamplingParams(temperature=0.0, max_tokens=max_new_tokens)
    outputs = llm.chat(
        messages,
        sampling_params=params,
        chat_template_kwargs={"enable_thinking": False},   # answer directly; no reasoning trace
        use_tqdm=False,
    )
    return outputs[0].outputs[0].text.strip()

print("Generator model and helper loaded.")

    6. The prompts

    call_qwen_chat has the signature the shared pipeline expects, generate(system_prompt, user_prompt, max_new_tokens) -> str, and embed_query has the other one. run_single_qa in wattbot_rag.py makes two calls per question with them:

    • The first asks for a JSON object with answer, answer_value (normalized scalar, range or category), answer_unit, ref_id (list of document ids), is_blank and supporting_materials. The retrieved chunks go in the user turn, labelled [doc_id, page N] so the model can cite them, along with the expected answer_unit from train_QA.csv as a hint, so the number comes back in the unit the ground truth uses.
    • The second, made only when the first produced an answer, asks for a short explanation. With with_evidence_type=True it also asks the model to name the main type of evidence (text, table, figure, or a combination) in the strict format evidence_type: explanation, and the code turns that into [evidence_type] explanation for the CSV, so the tag is parsed, not trusted.

    PYTHON 

    print(ANSWER_SYSTEM_PROMPT)
print("-" * 80)
print(explanation_system_prompt(with_evidence_type=True))

    7. Run over the full WattBot training set

    For every row of train_QA.csv, run_single_qa:

    1. Embeds the question and retrieves the top-k chunks.
    2. Asks Qwen for the answer JSON and parses it (a malformed reply counts as unanswerable).
    3. Decides answerability with a hybrid rule. The question is is_blank if the model said so or the top retrieval cosine score is below retrieval_threshold. Weak retrieval means the model is about to answer from memory instead of the papers, which is what RAG exists to prevent. A lower threshold marks fewer questions unanswerable, a higher one more; change it, rerun, and rescore to see the trade-off.
    4. Copies answer_unit from the row (never guessed), maps each ref_id to its URL via metadata.csv, and makes the explanation call.
    5. Returns one submission-format row; we collect them into train_solutions_qwen.csv.

    PYTHON 

    docid_to_url = build_docid_to_url(metadata_df)
from wattbot_rag import drop_questions_without_papers
train_df = drop_questions_without_papers(train_df, {d["doc_id"] for d in chunked_docs})   # as in the other RAG episodes: questions citing papers the corpus lacks are not scored

all_results = []
max_N = np.inf   # set to e.g. 5 for a smoke test
run_start = time.time()

for idx, row in train_df.iterrows():
    if idx >= max_N:
        break
    print("#" * 96)
    print(f"QUESTION: {row['question']}")

    res = run_single_qa(
        row=row,
        embed_query=embed_query,             # the embedding model on this GPU
        generate=call_qwen_chat,             # the vLLM engine on this GPU; the Bedrock episode passed its converse wrapper here
        chunk_embeddings=chunk_embeddings,
        chunked_docs=chunked_docs,
        docid_to_url=docid_to_url,
        top_k=8,
        retrieval_threshold=0.25,
        with_evidence_type=True,             # ask the explanation call to tag [text], [table], [figure]
        verbose=True,
    )
    print(f"ANSWER: {res['answer']}")
    print(f"ref_ids: {res['ref_id']}")
    print(f"EXPLANATION: {res['explanation']}")
    all_results.append(res)

solutions_df = pd.DataFrame(all_results)
print(f"Answered {len(solutions_df)} questions in {(time.time() - run_start) / 60:.1f} min on the notebook GPU")
solutions_path = os.path.join(local_data_dir, "train_solutions_qwen.csv")
solutions_df.to_csv(solutions_path, index=False)

print(f"Saved solutions for {len(solutions_df)} questions to: {solutions_path}")
solutions_df.head(20)

    Compare answers to ground truth

    WattBot scores each prediction with the competition’s own Score.py, 0.75 for answer_value (numeric within ±0.1% relative tolerance, categorical match after normalisation, zero if you answer a question the corpus cannot answer), 0.20 for citation F1 against the ground-truth ref_id set, and 0.05 for a clean refusal when the answer is is_blank. compute_wattbot_score from wattbot_rag.py calls it for the headline number, adds a per-row score, and prints the worst rows with the model’s explanation.

    PYTHON 

    results_df = compute_wattbot_score(
    train_qa_path=train_qa_path,
    preds_path=solutions_path,
    n_examples=10,
)

    Change retrieval_threshold or top_k in the loop above, rerun it, and rescore. With the model loaded, a pass over all 245 questions takes tens of minutes, and a max_N of 50 a few. Then stop the instance.

    Recap and next steps

    In this episode, we:

    • Pulled the WattBot corpus chunks that the Bedrock episode cached on S3 into our notebook environment, and reused the pipeline code (wattbot_rag.py) from the Bedrock and Processing Jobs episodes unchanged.
    • Created vector embeddings for each chunk and used similarity search to retrieve relevant context for a given question.
    • Used an LLM to generate answers from retrieved context and wrote results out to a CSV for later scoring and analysis.
    • Handled unanswerable questions with an is_blank flag so the system can explicitly say “I don’t know” when the evidence isn’t there.

    This is a first pass at a RAG pipeline. Next steps, in rough order of what they usually gain:

    • Stronger models: a larger or domain-tuned embedding model, or a more capable generator, if the GPU budget allows.

    • Add a reranking step: Instead of sending the top-k raw nearest neighbors directly to the LLM, use a cross-encoder or reranker model to re-score those candidates and send only the best ones.

    • Handle figures and tables more carefully: Many key numbers live in tables, figure captions, or plots. Consider:

      • OCR / table-parsing tools (e.g., pytesseract, table extractors, PDF parsers).
      • Multimodal models that can embed or interpret figures and diagrams, not just text.
      • Separate chunking strategies for captions, tables, and main text.

    • Enrich chunks with metadata: Attach metadata like section headings (e.g., Methods, Results), paper ID, year, or paragraph type. You can:

      • Filter or boost chunks by metadata at retrieval time.
      • Use metadata in the prompt so the LLM knows where evidence is coming from.

    • Models tuned on scientific text (arXiv, PubMed), which read equations and technical language more reliably and invent less when the prose is dense.

    Models, retrieval and preprocessing can each be swapped without changing the rest of the pipeline.

    The Processing Jobs episode does the same work, with the same wattbot_rag.py, as short-lived SageMaker jobs, so the GPU only bills while it is embedding or generating. Stop this instance now, and delete it if you are done with the episode.

    Key Points
    • Why self-host at all: Bedrock’s catalog is curated and lags releases; most open-weight models (including Qwen3.8-27B) are not on it. When the model you need is not offered, you rent a GPU and serve it yourself.
    • Inference uses reduced-precision weights: no gradients means the weights are the memory cost. FP8 puts a 27B model on one 48 GB GPU (ml.g6e.xlarge); bf16 would need 54 GB, an 80 GB GPU or a multi-GPU instance.
    • The meter never stops on its own: ml.g6e.xlarge is $2.61/h, $167 per forgotten weekend, $1,906 per forgotten month, plus $14/month for the storage volume even when stopped. Stop it when you stand up; delete it when the episode is over.
    • Retrieval is a matrix multiply: cosine similarity over the in-memory embedding matrix is enough for a corpus this size; a vector database is the same step for a corpus of millions.
    • Units come from the data: answer_unit is copied from train_QA.csv, never guessed by the model.
    • Two calls per question: one answers and cites; a second, shorter one writes the explanation and names the evidence type.
    • The competition’s format: is_blank marks unanswerable questions and missing fields, as the scorer expects.

    Content from (Optional) The Same Jobs from the Terminal

    Last updated on 2026-10-28 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 30 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What does the AWS command-line interface (CLI) let me do that the lesson’s notebooks did, and what should I not do with it?
    • How do I see, and stop, everything that is costing money from a terminal?
    • What request does the SageMaker SDK send when I call estimator.fit()?

    Objectives

    • Authenticate the CLI with short-lived Identity Center credentials, never with access keys.
    • List, inspect, and stop training jobs, processing jobs, tuning jobs and notebook instances from the terminal.
    • Copy data to and from S3 in bulk with aws s3 sync.
    • Launch one training job from its JSON description and recognise it as the request the SDK built in the training episodes.
    • State which resources the lesson never creates from the CLI, and why the account refuses them.

    Optional, self-study episode

    Everything in this lesson went through the SageMaker Python SDK in a notebook. The same account can be used from a terminal with the AWS CLI: to check on a job from another machine, to stop something when no notebook is open, to copy results out of S3 in bulk, or to script a launch. This episode does five things from a laptop terminal: signs in to the account with Identity Center, lists what is running and reads what a job cost, stops jobs and notebook instances, copies data to and from S3, and launches one training job from a JSON file, the same request estimator.fit() sent in the training episodes.

    The case for the terminal is the notebook instance. Every job in this lesson was launched from an ml.t3.medium that bills while it is on, five cents an hour, a dollar a day, and that someone has to remember to stop. A job launched from a laptop needs no instance at all: the request goes from your terminal to SageMaker, the job runs on a machine rented for it and ends, and the model lands in S3. For a project that launches a job a day and otherwise works locally, that is the notebook’s whole cost gone and nothing left running overnight. The training episode’s wait=False pattern gets most of the way there from a notebook; the CLI gets the rest.

    What you give up is what the instance did for you. On the instance, its role signs every call, the lesson’s helper checks a launch against the account’s rules before it goes, and the console shows what you started next to everyone else’s work. On a laptop you sign in yourself, the JSON carries no price and no check, and a mistake is not seen until the bill. The rules in the callout and the request check in section 5 cover that.

    Callout

    Read this before the first command

    The CLI, the SDK and the console are the same API. Nothing here is more powerful than a notebook cell. The difference is that a terminal shows nothing unless you ask: a notebook instance left running is visible in the console the next day, while an endpoint created from a terminal on a Friday is not noticed until the bill arrives. A past participant of this workshop spent a large share of a year’s credits that way. Three rules apply on the shared account and are worth keeping on your own:

    1. Authenticate with aws sso login only. Never aws configure with an access key ID and secret. Those are long-lived, and they end up in shell histories and committed files.
    2. Launch only jobs (training, processing, tuning), with the same three tags and the same MaxRuntimeInSeconds the notebooks always set. Jobs end on their own. Endpoints, EC2 instances and GPU notebook instances do not, and the lesson never creates them from the CLI, or at all.
    3. A refused create command is the account’s rules, not a fault. The workshop account carries a guard-rail policy that denies endpoint and EC2 creation, instance types outside the lesson’s list, caps over 48 hours, and any job whose three tags are missing, blank or off the Project and Purpose lists. Do not look for a workaround. The policy is on the notebook role today, which covers every launch from an instance; a laptop CLI runs under the permission set, which gets the same policy when the Identity Center administrator attaches it, and until then these rules are yours to keep by hand from a laptop. (Instructors: the policy and its status are on the Account preparation checklist page.)

    1. Sign in with Identity Center

    This episode runs from your own laptop, a terminal that works when no notebook is open. The AWS CLI is already installed in CloudShell and on every SageMaker notebook instance, where it uses the instance’s role and needs no sign-in; a laptop has neither, so install AWS CLI v2 there, then register the account’s Identity Center once. It asks four things. First the start URL and the region of the Identity Center sign-in page, the same ones you used in the browser; for the workshop account both are in the sign-in email from your instructor. It then opens a browser tab for you to approve the device, lets you pick the account and the permission set, and finally asks for a default region, us-east-2 for the workshop account, and a name for the profile.

    BASH 

    aws configure sso

    The commands in this episode are the same in Bash (macOS, Linux, Git Bash on Windows) and in PowerShell; where the shell’s own syntax differs, variables, line continuation, writing a file, the two are shown as tabs.

    From then on, every session starts with a login, and a check that you are who you think you are, in the account you think you are in:

    BASH 

    aws sso login --profile workshop
export AWS_PROFILE=workshop
aws sts get-caller-identity

    POWERSHELL 

    aws sso login --profile workshop
$env:AWS_PROFILE = "workshop"
aws sts get-caller-identity

    The output names the account ID and an AWSReservedSSO_... role. The credentials expire after a few hours; aws sso login again when a command returns ExpiredToken. Nothing that would still work next month is written anywhere.

    If you are on the notebook instance’s own terminal (JupyterLab, File → New → Terminal), skip this step: the instance’s role is already the identity, which is the reason the lesson works from one.

    2. What is running, and what a job cost

    The SageMaker SDK calls you used map one-to-one onto aws sagemaker subcommands. --query is a JMESPath filter that keeps the output to what you asked about.

    BASH 

    # Everything that is running right now, by type. Each list should be short, or empty.
aws sagemaker list-training-jobs   --status-equals InProgress --query 'TrainingJobSummaries[].TrainingJobName'
aws sagemaker list-processing-jobs --status-equals InProgress --query 'ProcessingJobSummaries[].ProcessingJobName'
aws sagemaker list-hyper-parameter-tuning-jobs --status-equals InProgress --query 'HyperParameterTuningJobSummaries[].HyperParameterTuningJobName'
aws sagemaker list-notebook-instances --query 'NotebookInstances[].[NotebookInstanceName,NotebookInstanceStatus,InstanceType]' --output table
aws sagemaker list-endpoints       # must print an empty list on the workshop account

    describe-training-job is the call behind job_cost_report() in the training episodes. The same number is there: billable time, which includes the container pull and data download you paid for.

    BASH 

    JOB=<a training job name from the list above>
aws sagemaker describe-training-job --training-job-name $JOB \
  --query '{status:TrainingJobStatus, instance:ResourceConfig.InstanceType, count:ResourceConfig.InstanceCount, billable_s:BillableTimeInSeconds}'

    POWERSHELL 

    $JOB = "<a training job name from the list above>"
aws sagemaker describe-training-job --training-job-name $JOB `
  --query '{status:TrainingJobStatus, instance:ResourceConfig.InstanceType, count:ResourceConfig.InstanceCount, billable_s:BillableTimeInSeconds}'

    Cost is billable seconds × instance count × the hourly rate, exactly as in the notebooks. Tags are returned by a separate call, which is also how you find the untagged job that shows on the bill under “No tag key”:

    BASH 

    ARN=$(aws sagemaker describe-training-job --training-job-name $JOB --query TrainingJobArn --output text)
aws sagemaker list-tags --resource-arn $ARN --query 'Tags[].[Key,Value]' --output table

    POWERSHELL 

    $ARN = aws sagemaker describe-training-job --training-job-name $JOB --query TrainingJobArn --output text
aws sagemaker list-tags --resource-arn $ARN --query 'Tags[].[Key,Value]' --output table

    3. Stopping jobs and notebook instances

    Each of these stops a charge.

    BASH 

    aws sagemaker stop-training-job   --training-job-name   <name>
aws sagemaker stop-processing-job --processing-job-name <name>
aws sagemaker stop-hyper-parameter-tuning-job --hyper-parameter-tuning-job-name <name>   # stops every child job
aws sagemaker stop-notebook-instance --notebook-instance-name <name>

    A stopped job keeps its logs and whatever it had already written to S3; a stopped notebook instance keeps /home/ec2-user/SageMaker/. Deleting an instance when you are done with it is the step that stops the storage charge too:

    BASH 

    aws sagemaker delete-notebook-instance --notebook-instance-name <name>   # only after it reports Stopped

    4. Copying to and from S3

    The S3 episode uploaded through the console and the SDK. For many files, or for pulling a job’s outputs down to a laptop, the CLI is the better tool:

    BASH 

    aws s3 ls s3://<your-bucket>/ --recursive --human-readable --summarize     # every object, and the bucket's total size
aws s3 sync s3://<your-bucket>/xgboost/ ./xgboost-outputs/                 # download a prefix; only new or changed files move
aws s3 sync ./my-data/ s3://<your-bucket>/my-data/                         # upload a folder the same way
aws s3 rm s3://<your-bucket>/scratch/ --recursive                          # delete a prefix; this one asks no questions

    Downloads to a laptop are a transfer out of AWS ($0.09 per GB). For anything larger than a few hundred megabytes, keep the data in the region and let a job read it, which is the lesson’s pattern.

    5. Launching a training job from a JSON file

    Every estimator.fit() in the training episodes assembled a JSON request and sent it to CreateTrainingJob. Here is that request. Fill in the placeholders from your notebook: the image URI (run print(xgboost_estimator.training_image_uri()) in the training episode’s notebook), your role ARN (print(role)), your bucket, your tag values, and a job name, which must be unique in the account.

    The request is a JSON file. Save it as train-xgboost.json with any editor, or from the shell:

    BASH 

    cat > train-xgboost.json <<'JSON'
{
  "TrainingJobName": "<notebook-instance-name>-cli-xgboost-1",
  "AlgorithmSpecification": {
    "TrainingImage": "<xgboost image URI for your region>",
    "TrainingInputMode": "File"
  },
  "RoleArn": "<execution role ARN>",
  "HyperParameters": { "objective": "binary:logistic", "num_round": "100", "max_depth": "5", "eta": "0.1" },
  "InputDataConfig": [
    {
      "ChannelName": "train",
      "ContentType": "text/csv",
      "DataSource": { "S3DataSource": {
        "S3DataType": "S3Prefix",
        "S3Uri": "s3://<your-bucket>/xgboost/builtin/train_builtin.csv",
        "S3DataDistributionType": "FullyReplicated" } }
    }
  ],
  "OutputDataConfig": { "S3OutputPath": "s3://<your-bucket>/xgboost/cli-output/" },
  "ResourceConfig": { "InstanceType": "ml.m5.large", "InstanceCount": 1, "VolumeSizeInGB": 10 },
  "StoppingCondition": { "MaxRuntimeInSeconds": 1200 },
  "Tags": [
    { "Key": "Project", "Value": "<ChallengeName>" },
    { "Key": "Name",    "Value": "<LastnameFirstname>" },
    { "Key": "Purpose", "Value": "Training" }
  ]
}
JSON

    POWERSHELL 

    @'
{
  "TrainingJobName": "<notebook-instance-name>-cli-xgboost-1",
  "AlgorithmSpecification": {
    "TrainingImage": "<xgboost image URI for your region>",
    "TrainingInputMode": "File"
  },
  "RoleArn": "<execution role ARN>",
  "HyperParameters": { "objective": "binary:logistic", "num_round": "100", "max_depth": "5", "eta": "0.1" },
  "InputDataConfig": [
    {
      "ChannelName": "train",
      "ContentType": "text/csv",
      "DataSource": { "S3DataSource": {
        "S3DataType": "S3Prefix",
        "S3Uri": "s3://<your-bucket>/xgboost/builtin/train_builtin.csv",
        "S3DataDistributionType": "FullyReplicated" } }
    }
  ],
  "OutputDataConfig": { "S3OutputPath": "s3://<your-bucket>/xgboost/cli-output/" },
  "ResourceConfig": { "InstanceType": "ml.m5.large", "InstanceCount": 1, "VolumeSizeInGB": 10 },
  "StoppingCondition": { "MaxRuntimeInSeconds": 1200 },
  "Tags": [
    { "Key": "Project", "Value": "<ChallengeName>" },
    { "Key": "Name",    "Value": "<LastnameFirstname>" },
    { "Key": "Purpose", "Value": "Training" }
  ]
}
'@ | Set-Content -Path train-xgboost.json

    Before sending it, check it the way the notebooks did. The lesson repository has the account’s rules in scripts/guardrails.json and a script that applies them to a request file; a Project or Purpose off the lists, an instance type off the list or a cap over 48 hours is named here, where AWS would refuse it silently:

    BASH 

    git clone -q https://github.com/carpentries-incubator/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker.git   # once, anywhere on the laptop
python ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts/check_request.py train-xgboost.json

    Then send it. This one line is estimator.fit():

    BASH 

    aws sagemaker create-training-job --cli-input-json file://train-xgboost.json

    Three fields to notice. StoppingCondition.MaxRuntimeInSeconds is the max_run you set on every estimator; the SDK would have sent 24 hours if you had not. Tags is the tags= argument; without it the request is refused when sent from a notebook instance, and nothing checks it from a laptop until the permission set carries the policy. ResourceConfig sets the instance type and count, which determine the cost; nothing in a JSON file prints a price, so look the type up on the Instances for ML page before sending it, as you would in a notebook.

    The CLI returns the moment the request is accepted; nothing waits. To follow the job the way wait=True did:

    BASH 

    aws sagemaker wait training-job-completed-or-stopped --training-job-name <the job name>   # blocks until it ends
aws sagemaker describe-training-job --training-job-name <the job name> --query '{status:TrainingJobStatus, billable_s:BillableTimeInSeconds, failure:FailureReason}'

    Estimate first, compare after, as always: this is the same ~4 minutes billable on ml.m5.large, about a cent.

    Callout

    What the lesson never does from the CLI

    • aws sagemaker create-endpoint / create-endpoint-config: an endpoint is a server that runs until you delete it, with no runtime cap. The lesson serves models with processing jobs and Bedrock so that nothing of this kind exists in the account.
    • aws sagemaker create-notebook-instance with a GPU type: a GPU notebook is $60 a day while you are asleep. The optional GPU-notebook episode creates one through the console, where it stays visible, and deletes it the same session.
    • aws ec2 run-instances: bare virtual machines have no tags required, no runtime cap and no SageMaker job list to appear in.

    On the workshop account all three are denied on the notebook role, as is any instance type outside the lesson’s list, any cap over 48 hours and any job whose tags are missing or off the lists; the permission set a laptop uses gets the same policy once the administrator attaches it. The instructor page Account preparation checklist has the policy. On your own account, the same denies are an afternoon’s work.

    Challenge

    Challenge: what is still running on Friday evening

    You are leaving for the weekend and have a terminal, not a browser. Write the commands you would run, in order, to make sure the account is costing nothing until Monday, and the one command to run if each check finds something. Then run them against your own resources.

    BASH 

    aws sso login --profile workshop && export AWS_PROFILE=workshop

    POWERSHELL 

    aws sso login --profile workshop; $env:AWS_PROFILE = "workshop"

    BASH 

    aws sagemaker list-training-jobs   --status-equals InProgress --query 'TrainingJobSummaries[].TrainingJobName'
aws sagemaker list-processing-jobs --status-equals InProgress --query 'ProcessingJobSummaries[].ProcessingJobName'
aws sagemaker list-hyper-parameter-tuning-jobs --status-equals InProgress --query 'HyperParameterTuningJobSummaries[].HyperParameterTuningJobName'
aws sagemaker list-notebook-instances --query 'NotebookInstances[?NotebookInstanceStatus==`InService`].NotebookInstanceName'
aws sagemaker list-endpoints --query 'Endpoints[].EndpointName'

    For anything the first four print: the matching stop-... command from section 3. A job you recognise as yours and expect to finish within its MaxRuntimeInSeconds can be left; a job you do not recognise is a question for its owner, and on a shared account the tags (list-tags) tell you who that is. For an endpoint: aws sagemaker delete-endpoint --endpoint-name <name>, then find out how it was created, because the notebook role refuses it and the permission set should once the policy is attached. Buckets cost almost nothing over a weekend and need no action.

    Key Points
    • The CLI, the SDK and the console are one API; the CLI shows you nothing you do not ask for, so its first use is to look and to stop, not to launch.
    • Authenticate with aws sso login and short-lived credentials; never store an access key.
    • list-*, describe-* and stop-* for training, processing and tuning jobs and notebook instances cover almost every reason to open a terminal.
    • A create-training-job JSON is what estimator.fit() sent: the same tags, the same MaxRuntimeInSeconds, the same instance choice, with no price printed next to it.
    • Endpoints, EC2 instances and GPU notebooks are not jobs and do not end; the workshop account’s notebook role denies creating them, and your own account should too.

    Content from Resource Management and Monitoring

    Last updated on 2026-10-28 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 35 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How can I monitor and manage AWS resources to avoid unnecessary costs?
    • What steps are necessary to clean up SageMaker and S3 resources after the workshop?
    • What best practices can help with efficient resource utilization?

    Objectives

    • Understand how to shut down SageMaker notebook instances to minimize costs.
    • Clean up S3 storage and stop running jobs.
    • Explore basic resource management strategies and tools for AWS.

    Open the notebook from: /ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/notebooks/15_Resource-management-cleanup.ipynb. Any kernel works; conda_python3 is fine. This episode is mostly console steps, but the cells below ask AWS what is still running or stored under your name, so you can check the list against reality before and after you clean up.

    Initial setup

    PYTHON 

    import boto3
import sagemaker
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, "/home/ec2-user/SageMaker/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/scripts")   # the lesson's helper module, cloned in the controllers episode
import helpers

session = sagemaker.Session()
sm = session.sagemaker_client          # the low-level SageMaker client: list_*, describe_*, stop_* calls
region = session.boto_region_name      # the region the notebook runs in (us-east-2 on the workshop account)

name = "DoeJohn"                              # replace with your name, as used in job names and tags
project = "SinkOrSwim"   # the Project value used in your Bedrock profile names
bucket_name = "sinkorswim-doejohn"            # replace with your bucket

    What is still running under your name?

    One pass over the three job lists shows every job still running in the account; yours are the ones with your notebook name in the training jobs and the WattBot- Processing jobs you launched. A completed job holds nothing; an InProgress one bills until it ends or hits its cap.

    PYTHON 

    # Every notebook instance in the account (the list is shared, so other learners' instances appear too), with its status.
# InService bills the instance's hourly rate; Stopped bills only the volume.
print("Notebook instances (bill while InService; volume bills while Stopped):")
for nb in sm.list_notebook_instances()["NotebookInstances"]:
    print(f"  {nb['NotebookInstanceName']:<40} {nb['NotebookInstanceStatus']:<12} {nb['InstanceType']}")

# The three kinds of job, each with its own list call. The call returns a dictionary; the list of jobs is under a key
# whose name differs per kind ("TrainingJobSummaries", ...), and so does the key holding the job's name, so the loop
# carries both. StatusEquals keeps only running jobs; NameContains keeps the ones with your name in the job name.
print("\nJobs still InProgress in the account:")
running = 0
for kind, lister, key, name_key in [
    ("training",   sm.list_training_jobs,              "TrainingJobSummaries",            "TrainingJobName"),
    ("tuning",     sm.list_hyper_parameter_tuning_jobs, "HyperParameterTuningJobSummaries", "HyperParameterTuningJobName"),
    ("processing", sm.list_processing_jobs,            "ProcessingJobSummaries",          "ProcessingJobName"),
]:
    for job in lister(StatusEquals="InProgress", MaxResults=50)[key]:   # every running job in the account; the Processing jobs are not named after you, so no name filter
        print(f"  {kind:<11} {job[name_key]}")
        running += 1
print("  none" if running == 0 else f"  {running} job(s) still billing: stop them from the console if you no longer need them")

    Then storage, which bills whether or not anything runs:

    PYTHON 

    helpers.get_s3_bucket_size(bucket_name)   # sums the size of every object in the bucket; S3 bills per GB-month whether or not anything runs

    And the Bedrock inference profiles, which cost nothing to keep but are yours to remove (the instructors’ cleanup does not touch them):

    PYTHON 

    bedrock = boto3.client("bedrock", region_name=region)   # the Bedrock control-plane client: profiles are created and deleted here, not on the runtime client
mine = f"{project}-{name}-"   # the Bedrock episode named every profile <project>-<name>-<label>, so this prefix is yours and nobody else's
# list_inference_profiles returns every application profile in the account; keep the ones whose name starts with your prefix
profiles = [p for p in bedrock.list_inference_profiles(typeEquals="APPLICATION")["inferenceProfileSummaries"]
            if p["inferenceProfileName"].startswith(mine)]
for p in profiles:
    print(p["inferenceProfileName"], p["inferenceProfileArn"])   # the ARN is what the delete call below takes
print("none" if not profiles else f"{len(profiles)} profile(s) with your prefix; the next cell deletes them")

    Deleting them is one call per profile. The cell deletes only the profiles the cell above listed, the ones whose name starts with your project and your name, so nobody else’s are touched even though the account’s policy would allow it; read the list before you set the flag.

    PYTHON 

    confirm_delete = False   # set to True after reading the list above

if confirm_delete:
    for p in profiles:   # only the profiles the cell above listed: yours, by prefix
        bedrock.delete_inference_profile(inferenceProfileIdentifier=p["inferenceProfileArn"])   # one call per profile; there is no undo
        print("deleted", p["inferenceProfileName"])
    profiles = []        # so a rerun of this cell does not try to delete them twice
else:
    print("nothing deleted; set confirm_delete = True and rerun to delete the profiles listed above")

    Now the console steps. Rerun the cells above when you are done; every list should be empty or Stopped.

    Shutting down notebook instances

    Notebook instances bill per second at an hourly rate while they run, so stop or delete them when they are no longer needed. Earlier in the Notebooks as controllers episode, we discussed using lower-cost instance types like ml.t3.medium (approximately $0.05/hour) for controlling workflows. A small instance left running still bills a dollar a day.

    1. Navigate to SageMaker in the AWS Console.
    2. In the left-hand menu, click Notebook instances.
    3. Locate your notebook instance and select it.
    4. Choose Stop to shut it down temporarily or Delete to permanently remove it. > Tip: If you plan to reuse the notebook later, stopping it is sufficient. Deleting is recommended if you are finished with the workshop.

    A stopped instance stops the compute charge but keeps its storage volume, which bills at about $0.14 per GB-month. The 20 GB the controllers episode set is $2.80 a month; the 100 GB volume the optional GPU-notebook episode asks for is $14 a month. If you enlarged the volume to hold model weights, delete the instance once the episode is done.

    Cleaning up S3 storage

    S3 storage is cheap, and a bucket left behind bills every month until it is deleted.

    1. Navigate to the S3 Console.
    2. Locate the bucket(s) you created for this workshop.
    3. Open the bucket and select any objects (files) you no longer need.
    4. Click Delete to remove the selected objects.
    5. To delete an entire bucket:
      • Empty the bucket by selecting Empty bucket under Bucket actions.
      • Delete the bucket by clicking Delete bucket.

    Reminder: Earlier in the workshop, we set up tags for S3 buckets. Use these tags to filter and identify workshop-related buckets, so that only workshop resources are deleted.

    Monitoring and stopping active jobs

    SageMaker charges for training, tuning and Processing jobs while they run, so stop jobs you no longer need. Every job in this lesson was launched with a runtime cap (max_run on training and tuning jobs, max_runtime_in_seconds on Processing jobs), so a forgotten job ends on its own.

    1. In the SageMaker Console, go to Training jobs, Hyperparameter tuning jobs, or Processing jobs.
    2. Identify any active jobs that you no longer need.
    3. Select the jobs and click Stop. > Tip: Review the job logs to ensure you’ve saved the results before stopping a job.

    Billing and cost monitoring

    To see what you are spending:

    1. Set up billing alerts:
      • Go to the AWS Billing Dashboard.
      • Navigate to Budgets and create a budget alert to track your spending.
    2. Review usage and costs:
      • Use the AWS Cost Explorer in the Billing Dashboard to view detailed expenses by service, such as SageMaker and S3. To turn a line on the bill back into hours, the rates are on the Instances for ML page.
    3. Use tags for cost tracking:
      • Refer to the tags you set up earlier in the workshop. Remember that tags never propagate between resources: your notebook instance, each S3 bucket, each training/tuning/Processing job, and each Bedrock application inference profile carries its own tags, and anything you launched without tags is untraceable after the fact.
      • Only the three approved keys count on the bill, Name, Project and Purpose, spelled exactly (the S3 episode says why); a tag you just added can take up to 24 hours to appear in Cost Explorer.
      • Bedrock application inference profiles cost nothing to keep, but delete the ones you created once a project is finished; the cells at the top of this episode do it for the ones carrying your name.

    End-of-workshop checklist

    Work through this list before you sign off for the last time.

    • Notebook instances: Stop, then Delete (SageMaker → Notebook instances). Includes the optional GPU notebook instance if you created one.
    • S3 bucket: empty and delete your challenge-lastnamefirstname bucket (S3 → select bucket → Empty, then Delete). Download anything you want to keep first, once: egress is $0.09/GB. Leave the shared data bucket alone; it is the instructors’.
    • Default SDK bucket sagemaker-<region>-<account-id>: created automatically the first time a job staged its code. In the shared account the instructors delete it; on your own account, empty and delete it with the rest.
    • Training, tuning and Processing jobs: confirm none are still running (SageMaker → each job list, filter by status InProgress). Completed jobs hold no billable resource; their artifacts are in your bucket and go with it.
    • Bedrock application inference profiles: delete the ones you created, with the two cells at the top of this episode (they list and delete only the profiles named with your project and your name) or from the Bedrock console.
    • GitHub personal access token: revoke it on GitHub (Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens) if you made one for the optional PAT episode.

    Every stop and delete in this list has a one-line CLI equivalent; the optional episode The Same Jobs from the Terminal collects them, for stopping something from a machine with no browser.

    In the shared workshop account, the instructors sweep the account with aws-nuke after the workshop. That sweep deletes notebook instances and the learner buckets only, so if you forget those, they will still go. It does not touch Bedrock application inference profiles, so those are yours to remove.

    Rules the account enforces, and how to set them on your own

    Several things you could have done wrong in this workshop were refused before they cost anything: a job launched without the three tags, with a blank name, with a Project that is not on the account’s list, with an instance type outside the lesson’s list, a Processing job with no runtime cap, and any endpoint or EC2 instance at all. None of that is SageMaker’s own behaviour. It is a set of rules the account administrator attached to the role your notebook runs as, written in the same IAM policy language that gave the role its permissions, and each one says: refuse this request if it looks like this. An AWS account with no such rules lets a tagged job and an untagged one through alike, and lets a notebook instance run until someone remembers it.

    If you administer an account of your own, a lab’s or a project’s, the same rules are an afternoon’s work, and they hold across the console, the SDK and the CLI, because all three are the same API. The lesson’s Account preparation checklist instructor page has the policy as JSON and the one command that attaches it to a role; its Overnight safeguards section has the three measures that go with it. In order of what they prevent for what they cost:

    Rule What it stops How it is done
    Every job carries the three cost tags, with real values spend nobody can attribute an IAM deny on CreateTrainingJob and the like when aws:RequestTag/Name is missing or blank, or Project and Purpose are missing or not on their lists
    Only instance types you have priced the $63-an-hour box chosen by accident an IAM deny when sagemaker:InstanceTypes is not on your list
    A runtime cap on every job, at most 48 hours a hung job billing for a week an IAM deny when sagemaker:MaxRuntimeInSeconds is missing or too large
    No endpoints, no EC2 the two resource kinds with no runtime cap at all an IAM deny on CreateEndpoint and ec2:RunInstances
    Notebook instances stop at 11 pm the forgotten GPU notebook, $63 a night a ten-line scheduled Lambda function
    A budget per person and a brake on the total a quiet overspend AWS Budgets on the Name tag, with an action that attaches a deny policy at the ceiling

    A deny applies to everyone who uses the role, including you, so your own launches need real tag values and listed instance types too. And the error a refused request gets, AccessDeniedException ... with an explicit deny in an identity-based policy, does not say which rule matched, so write the rules down where the people using the account will find them. A deny cannot carry a custom message either: AWS says explicit deny in an identity-based policy and nothing more, which is why this lesson keeps a copy of the policy next to its helper code and checks every launch against it in the notebook first, with helpers.check_launch, so the message you get names the rule. The If a Launch Is Refused page is the same list in one place, for the day a job of your own is refused.

    What you can do without an administrator:

    • Automate the cleanup you do by hand. The inventory cells at the top of this episode are the SDK calls; a script that runs them and stops what it finds is the Lambda in the table above.
    • Test on a slice first. Every expensive run in this lesson was preceded by a small one on the same code: a few epochs, a subset of pages, a handful of questions.
    • Estimate, then compare. Write down what a run should cost before launching it, read BillableTimeInSeconds afterwards, and find out why when the two disagree, as the fine-tuning episode does.
    • Tag everything, yourself, every time. Cost allocation tags are the only way a shared bill becomes individual bills, and they never propagate.
    Challenge

    Challenge: your own cleanup list

    Without looking at the checklist above, list every billable resource you created in this workshop, and for each one write down where it is deleted (which console page, or which command). Then compare with the checklist. Which items would have kept billing if you had only stopped your notebook instance and walked away?

    A complete list for someone who did every episode, including the optional ones:

    Resource Created in Bills while it exists? Where it is deleted
    S3 bucket challenge-lastnamefirstname and everything in it (the Titanic files and .npz arrays at the root, and the docs/, xgboost/, output_nn/, wattbot/ and badger-scribe/ prefixes) S3 episode Yes: storage per GB-month S3 console → Empty bucket → Delete bucket
    The SDK’s default bucket sagemaker-<region>-<account-id> (code tarballs staged by every fit() and run()) Training episode, automatically Yes, a little: storage per GB-month, shared by the whole account Instructors delete it at the end of term; on your own account, empty and delete it like any other bucket
    Controller notebook instance (ml.t3.medium) Notebooks as controllers Yes while InService; its volume bills while Stopped SageMaker → Notebook instances → Stop → Delete
    Training jobs (XGBoost, PyTorch), tuning jobs, Processing jobs Training, tuning, RAG and fine-tuning episodes Only while running; all capped by max_run / max_runtime_in_seconds SageMaker → job lists → Stop if InProgress; nothing to delete afterwards
    Bedrock application inference profiles RAG on Bedrock No (the calls billed per token when made) The delete cell at the top of this episode, or the Bedrock console
    GPU notebook instance (ml.g6e.xlarge, 100 GB volume) Optional GPU-notebook episode Yes: $2.61/h InService, $14/month for the volume when Stopped SageMaker → Notebook instances → Delete
    GitHub personal access token Optional PAT episode No, but it is a credential GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → revoke

    Stopping the controller and walking away leaves the bucket billing for storage, a stopped GPU instance’s volume billing at $0.14/GB-month, and any Processing job that had not hit its max_runtime_in_seconds yet. Model artifacts in your bucket are the only thing worth keeping; download them once, then delete the bucket.

    Key Points

    • Always stop or delete notebook instances when not in use to avoid charges.

    • Stop any training, tuning or Processing job you no longer need.

    • Bedrock application inference profiles are not swept by the instructors’ aws-nuke run; remove them yourself.

    • The refusals you met in this workshop (untagged jobs, wrong instance types, endpoints) are IAM deny rules an administrator attached to the role, not SageMaker defaults; on an account you administer, the instructor pages have the policy to copy.

    • Regularly clean up unused S3 buckets and objects to save on storage costs.

    • Monitor your expenses through the AWS Billing Dashboard and set up alerts.

    • Use tags (set up earlier in the workshop) to track and monitor costs by resource.
